lessons.title: The Boom: Consumerism, Mass Production and Republican Policy
lessons.description: How tariffs, hire purchase and the assembly line turned 1920s America into a consumer society.
lessons.content_html:
A Decade That Believed in Buying

In 1920 a Model T Ford cost a worker about three months’ wages. By 1925 the same car cost three weeks’ wages and could be bought on credit with no money down. America in the 1920s did not just produce more goods than ever before — it persuaded ordinary people that buying those goods was the modern, patriotic thing to do. The Republican presidents Warren Harding, Calvin Coolidge and Herbert Hoover kept government out of the way. Industry kept the assembly lines moving. Advertising kept the wallets opening.

Key Fact

Three Republican policies powered the Boom: laissez-faire (minimal government interference), high tariffs like the 1922 Fordney–McCumber Act (which protected US factories from foreign competition), and low taxation on the rich (which freed money to invest). All three favoured big business.

Henry Ford and the Assembly Line

Henry Ford did not invent the motor car, but he transformed how it was built. By breaking car assembly into small repeated tasks on a moving conveyor belt, his Highland Park plant cut the time to build a Model T from over twelve hours to ninety minutes. Mass production let Ford slash the price from $850 in 1908 to under $300 by 1925. By 1929 there were over twenty-six million cars on American roads — one for every five people.

The car industry pulled the rest of the economy with it. Steel, rubber, glass, leather and paint were all needed in huge quantities. New roads, petrol stations and roadside diners spread across the country. Suburbs grew as workers could now drive to factory jobs. Ford’s decision to pay his workers $5 a day — double the going rate — was good business: well-paid Ford workers could afford to buy Ford cars.

Hire Purchase and the Consumer Society

Mass production created mountains of goods; hire purchase made sure ordinary Americans could buy them. By 1929 about three quarters of cars and half of all household appliances — refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, washing machines, radios — were bought on credit. Department stores ran whole catalogues of items available for ‘a dollar down and a dollar a week’. Buying on credit became normal rather than shameful.

Spending on advertising in the USA roughly tripled in the 1920s, from around $1.4 billion to nearly $3 billion a year. Companies hired psychologists and used new techniques: bright colour magazine advertisements, glamorous endorsements from film stars and sports heroes, and radio jingles. Advertisers stopped describing what a product did and started selling what it would make you feel: modern, attractive, successful. Catalogue chains like Sears Roebuck mailed out millions of copies; the chain store Woolworth’s grew to over 1,500 branches.

Radio was central. The first commercial station, KDKA in Pittsburgh, began broadcasting in 1920; by 1929 there were 618 stations and ten million households owned a set. Adverts bought during popular evening shows reached more Americans in one night than a magazine could in a month.

Republican Government Policies

Laissez-faire was more than an idea; it was a deliberate strategy. Coolidge famously summed it up: ‘The chief business of the American people is business.’ Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon cut the top rate of income tax from 73% in 1921 to 25% by 1925, leaving the wealthy with money to invest in new factories and stocks. The Fordney–McCumber Tariff of 1922 raised import duties to record levels — foreign goods became expensive, so Americans bought home-made products. Trade unions were weakened: courts banned strikes, and the share of workers in unions fell.

Key Fact

The Fordney–McCumber Tariff (1922) raised import duties on foreign goods by an average of 38%. Combined with Mellon’s tax cuts for the rich, US factories sold more, profits rose sharply, and shareholders had more spare cash to plough into the stock market — setting up the Wall Street boom of Lesson 2.

By 1929 about one in twelve American workers had a job that depended directly on cars. Steel, rubber, glass, leather and paint were all demanded in record quantities. Petrol stations multiplied from a few hundred in 1920 to over 120,000 by 1929. New roads, motels and roadside diners spread along highways like Route 66 (laid out in 1926). Electrical industries grew almost as fast: the radio sector grew fourteen-fold, and refrigerator sales rose from 5,000 in 1921 to over 800,000 by 1929. New construction methods (steel framing, electric lifts) drove a skyscraper boom — the Chrysler Building was completed in 1930 and the Empire State Building in 1931. The Boom was a network of industries pulling on each other, not a single product.

A Cycle of Boom

For middle-class Americans the Boom looked like a virtuous circle. Mass production made goods cheap, advertising made them desirable, hire purchase made them affordable, low taxes left people with more money, and tariffs kept foreign rivals out. Wages for industrial workers rose by about 25% across the decade. New industries — cars, aircraft, electrical goods, chemicals — were the fastest growing in the world. By 1929 the USA produced 42% of the world’s manufactured goods.

But the cycle had a hidden assumption: that wages, credit and confidence would all keep climbing together. When historians later disagreed about whether the Boom was a genuine miracle or an unstable bubble, this is the debate they were having. Lesson 2 looks at the Wall Street side of that bubble — and at the Americans the Boom never reached.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question on the Boom, do not just list industries that grew — track the chain. A useful sentence pattern: ‘Mass production cut prices, which lifted demand, which encouraged firms to advertise more aggressively, which in turn normalised hire purchase.’ Examiner reports flag students who write a chronology of events; the marks are for showing how one effect produced the next. Always name a Republican policy by date (1922 Fordney–McCumber, 1924 Mellon tax cuts) rather than describing it vaguely as ‘the government helped business’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mass production, led by Ford’s assembly line, slashed the price of cars and consumer goods and made the motor industry the engine of the 1920s economy.
  • Hire purchase and a tripling of advertising spend turned American households into a consumer society where buying on credit became normal.
  • Republican policies of laissez-faire, the 1922 Fordney–McCumber Tariff and Mellon’s tax cuts protected and accelerated the Boom — but built it on rising debt and concentrated wealth.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of mass production in the American motor industry in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A moving assembly line at Ford’s Highland Park plant carried each car past stationary workers, each doing one repeated task — the time to build a Model T fell from over twelve hours to ninety minutes.
• Standardised parts were used across every Model T, so cars could be built quickly and repaired anywhere — Ford famously offered the Model T ‘in any colour, so long as it’s black’.
• Workers were paid $5 a day, double the going rate, so that they could afford to buy the cars they were making.
• Mass production was rolled out beyond cars to consumer goods such as refrigerators and radios, which dropped sharply in price across the decade.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature with detail]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did hire purchase and advertising drive the growth of the consumer society in 1920s America?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hire purchase let ordinary Americans buy expensive goods on credit — by 1929 about 75% of cars and 50% of household appliances were bought this way, multiplying demand far beyond what cash purchases could have produced.
• ‘A dollar down and a dollar a week’ schemes made middle-class consumption normal rather than shameful, removing the cultural brake on borrowing.
• Advertising spend tripled across the decade to nearly $3 billion a year; firms used psychology, film-star endorsements and bright colour magazine ads to sell feelings (modernity, glamour) rather than just products.
• Radio — from 1920’s KDKA Pittsburgh to 618 stations and ten million sets by 1929 — carried adverts into the home every evening, reaching audiences no print campaign could match.
• The two effects reinforced each other: advertising created the desire for the latest washing machine, hire purchase removed the obstacle to owning one, and the result was a self-sustaining consumer cycle.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation tracking how hire purchase and advertising fed the consumer society, with precise figures and a chain of effects.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail on both factors.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one factor or to description rather than effects.
Emerging: Identifies hire purchase or advertising without explaining their effect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two Republican government policies of the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Fordney–McCumber Tariff (1922) raised import duties on foreign manufactured goods by an average of around 38%, protecting US factories from European competition.
• Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon cut the top rate of income tax from 73% in 1921 to 25% by 1925, leaving wealthy Americans with more money to invest.
• Laissez-faire: presidents Harding, Coolidge and Hoover deliberately kept federal regulation of business to a minimum, summed up by Coolidge’s line that ‘the chief business of the American people is business’.
• Hostility to trade unions: courts banned strikes and union membership fell across the decade, keeping wages flexible for employers.

[4 marks — 2 marks per policy: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did Henry Ford change the American economy in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Ford’s moving assembly line at Highland Park cut Model T production time from over twelve hours to ninety minutes, dropping the price from $850 in 1908 to under $300 by 1925.
• By 1929 there were over 26 million cars on American roads — about one car for every five Americans — transforming travel and stimulating the demand for petrol, road-building and suburbs.
• The car industry pulled forward demand for steel, rubber, glass, leather and paint, making it the keystone industry of the decade.
• Ford’s $5-a-day wage policy raised expectations of working-class living standards and meant his own workers could buy his cars — demonstrating the link between high wages and high consumption.
• Mass production methods spread from Ford to other manufacturers (electrical goods, household appliances), turning the assembly line into the model of American industry.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of effects across multiple sectors with precise detail and a clear sense of how Ford’s methods reshaped the economy.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail on Ford’s impact.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description of the assembly line.
Emerging: Identifies Ford as important without explaining how he changed the economy.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on the Boom of the 1920s: mass production, or Republican government policies? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of mass production:
• Ford’s assembly line cut the cost of a Model T from $850 to under $300, making car ownership realistic for working families and pulling steel, rubber and glass with it.
• Mass production methods spread to refrigerators, radios and washing machines, creating the goods that the consumer society then bought.
• Without affordable goods, hire purchase and advertising would have had nothing to sell.

In support of Republican policies:
• The 1922 Fordney–McCumber Tariff shielded US factories from European competition, allowing prices and profits to rise.
• Mellon’s tax cuts (top rate from 73% to 25%) freed wealthy Americans’ money to invest in new factories and stocks.
• Laissez-faire allowed mass production techniques to be rolled out without regulation, child-labour disputes or worker protection.

Judgement: The strongest answers note that the two factors worked together — Republican policies created the protected, low-tax environment in which mass production techniques could be most profitable. A defensible verdict is that mass production was the engine but Republican policies were the fuel.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument weighing both factors, with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both factors but weighs them unevenly; judgement is asserted rather than substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each factor without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Fordney–McCumber Tariff and Mellon's tax cuts on the American economy in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The 1922 Fordney–McCumber Tariff raised average import duties on manufactured goods by around 38%, making foreign products expensive and encouraging Americans to buy from US factories.
• This protection meant domestic firms could maintain higher prices and profits, fuelling investment in new plant and machinery.
• Mellon cut the top rate of income tax from 73% in 1921 to 25% by 1925, leaving wealthy investors with billions more to channel into shares and corporate bonds.
• These freed funds drove the Wall Street boom; share prices rose steeply across the decade as the demand for stocks outpaced new issues.
• A side effect was inequality: high tariffs and low income tax rewarded shareholders far more than wage earners or farmers, who faced higher prices for everyday goods and shrinking export markets — a problem covered in Lesson 2.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects linking tariff and tax policy to investment, the stock market and inequality.
Secure: Clear explanation of effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one policy or to description.
Emerging: Identifies the policies without explaining their effects.

lessons.title: Wall Street Boom and the Inequalities Beneath It
lessons.description: The stock-market climb, speculation on the margin and the Americans the Boom left behind.
lessons.content_html:
A Bull Market and a Divided Country

If Lesson 1 explained how the Boom worked for middle-class buyers, Lesson 2 looks at where their money went and who was left out. Across the 1920s the Dow Jones industrial average climbed from 100 points in 1924 to 381 points in September 1929. Newspapers ran daily share-price columns; shoeshine boys offered tips. But while one third of Americans bought their first refrigerator, another third lived in homes without electricity. The Boom was loud at the top of society and silent at the bottom.

Key Fact

By 1929 around three million Americans owned shares, and most paid only 10% of the price up front, borrowing the rest from their stockbroker. This was called buying on the margin. It worked while prices were rising — but if shares fell, the loan still had to be repaid in full.

The Wall Street Boom

The Wall Street stock market boomed because three things happened at once. Republican tax cuts (Lesson 1) left wealthy Americans with billions to invest. Mass production was generating record corporate profits, so company shares looked like a sure bet. And new buying rules let small investors join in. The result was a rising stock market in which prices ran far ahead of the real value of the companies underneath.

Brokers offered buying on the margin as a way for ordinary Americans to take part. A clerk who put down $100 could borrow $900 to buy $1,000 of shares. If the shares rose to $1,500, he sold, repaid the $900 loan, and walked away with a $500 profit on his original $100. Speculators — people who bought shares to make a quick profit rather than to invest in a business — piled into the market. By 1929 the volume of margin loans had reached over $9 billion.

Speculation drove prices upward in a self-feeding loop. People bought shares because they were rising; the buying made them rise more; rising prices attracted yet more buyers. Newspapers printed stories of secretaries and lift operators making fortunes. By 1929 the Radio Corporation of America’s shares had risen 500% in two years, even though the company had paid no dividend. Investors were not buying a stake in a business; they were buying the chance to sell to someone else for more.

Most ordinary Americans never bought shares — only about 1.5 million of the country’s 30 million households did. But banks invested customers’ deposits in the market, so when share prices wobbled, the banks themselves were exposed. The whole edifice rested on the assumption that prices would only ever climb.

The Inequalities Beneath the Boom

The richest 5% of Americans took home one third of all national income in 1929. The poorest 40% received less than a sixth. The Boom benefited shareholders, business owners and skilled industrial workers. It largely bypassed the groups below.

Farmers and Sharecroppers

The First World War had been good for American farmers: European fighting wrecked French and German agriculture, so the USA exported huge surpluses of wheat and meat. After 1921 European production recovered and prices collapsed. Wheat prices fell from $2.50 a bushel in 1920 to under $1 by 1929. Six million American farmers were forced off their land across the decade. Mechanisation made matters worse — tractors meant fewer labourers were needed, and farm employment fell sharply.

Conditions were worst in the South. Sharecroppers — both white and black, but disproportionately African-American — rented land in exchange for half their crop. When cotton prices fell, sharecroppers could end the season owing the landlord more than they earned. Their incomes were a fraction of the national average and stayed there throughout the Boom.

African-Americans, Native Americans and Immigrants

In the southern states, Jim Crow laws kept African-Americans out of decent jobs, schools and voting booths. The Great Migration north to Chicago, Detroit and New York gave some families industrial wages, but they faced housing segregation and were the first to be sacked when work slowed. Native Americans, confined to reservations on poor land, lived in extreme poverty — the 1928 Meriam Report described conditions as a national disgrace. New immigrants from southern and eastern Europe were funnelled into the lowest-paid factory jobs and faced the immigration restrictions covered in Lesson 5.

Between 1916 and 1929 around 1.3 million African-Americans left the rural South for industrial cities like Chicago, Detroit, New York and Cleveland. They escaped the worst of Jim Crow segregation and could earn factory wages well above sharecropping incomes. But the welcome was conditional. Estate agents enforced ‘restrictive covenants’ that kept whole neighbourhoods white-only, so African-Americans were channelled into overcrowded districts like Harlem and Chicago’s South Side. Trade unions in many industries refused to admit black members, leaving them in the lowest-paid roles. White workers in some cities rioted when black migrants arrived — Chicago in 1919, Tulsa (Oklahoma) in 1921, where a thriving African-American business district called Greenwood was burned to the ground. The Great Migration was an opportunity, but it was an opportunity inside a country that was still deeply hostile.

Key Fact

The Boom left out farmers (collapsing crop prices), sharecroppers (debt to landlords), African-Americans (Jim Crow segregation), Native Americans (reservations) and unskilled industrial workers (whose wages rose far less than profits). For the unit’s analytical question — opportunity for whom, inequality for whom? — this list is the answer.

Why Two Halves of the Same Decade

Take the two halves of this lesson together. Wall Street was rising on borrowed money for a small minority. The countryside was sinking into debt for a much larger one. When the bubble burst in October 1929 (Lesson 6) it would not just hurt the speculators; it would hit a country whose foundations were already unequal. That is why historians remember the 1920s as a decade of opportunity AND inequality, not one or the other.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question on the Wall Street Boom, do not stop at ‘share prices rose’. Show three linked effects: investors borrowed on the margin, speculation pushed prices ahead of real company values, and banks became exposed when they invested customers’ deposits in the market. For the ‘opportunity and inequality’ analytical lens that runs through this whole unit, always answer the prompt ‘benefit for whom?’ with a named group (farmers, sharecroppers, African-Americans, Native Americans) and a specific cause — vague phrases like ‘some people did not benefit’ cap students at the lower bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street boom climbed steeply because tax cuts, corporate profits and buying on the margin (10% deposit, 90% broker loan) drew small investors into the market.
  • Speculation pushed share prices far ahead of company values, while banks invested customer deposits in the same shares — concentrating risk in the financial system.
  • Farmers, sharecroppers, African-Americans, Native Americans and unskilled workers were largely excluded from the Boom — making the 1920s a decade of both opportunity and deep inequality.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Wall Street stock market boom in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Share prices rose steeply — the Dow Jones industrial average climbed from 100 points in 1924 to 381 points in September 1929.
• Buying on the margin allowed investors to put down 10% of the price and borrow the rest from a broker; by 1929 margin loans totalled over $9 billion.
• Around three million Americans owned shares by 1929 — many for the first time — encouraged by newspaper tips and stories of overnight fortunes.
• Speculators bought shares not for long-term investment but to sell quickly at a higher price; companies like RCA saw share prices rise 500% in two years despite paying no dividend.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did buying on the margin and speculation reshape the American stock market in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Buying on the margin let ordinary Americans put down 10% of a share price and borrow the rest from a broker, opening the stock market to clerks and small savers who could never have paid in full.
• Margin loans rose to over $9 billion by 1929; the loans were repayable in full whatever happened to share prices, building large hidden risk into the system.
• Speculation — buying to resell quickly — meant prices rose because of demand from buyers, not because of company performance; RCA shares rose 500% in two years without paying any dividend.
• Banks invested customers’ deposits in the rising market, so a fall in share prices would directly hit the savings of millions of ordinary Americans who had never bought a share themselves.
• The combined effect was a self-feeding bubble: rising prices attracted buyers, whose buying lifted prices further — the structure that would collapse in October 1929 (Lesson 6).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from margin buying through speculation to systemic risk, with precise figures.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description rather than effects.
Emerging: Identifies margin or speculation without explaining their effects.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the position of farmers in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Wheat prices collapsed from $2.50 a bushel in 1920 to under $1 by 1929 as European agriculture recovered after the First World War.
• Around six million Americans were forced off their farms across the decade, often into debt.
• Mechanisation through tractors and combine harvesters meant farms needed fewer labourers, so rural employment fell sharply.
• Sharecroppers, particularly African-Americans in the South, rented land for half their crop and fell deeper into debt to landlords as cotton prices fell.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the 1920s Boom create inequality between different groups in American society?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The richest 5% of Americans took home a third of national income in 1929 while the poorest 40% received less than a sixth — the gap widened across the decade.
• Farm prices collapsed from 1921 onwards, while urban industrial profits grew; rural Americans fell further behind their city counterparts.
• Sharecroppers, often African-American, were locked into debt by falling cotton prices and could end seasons owing the landlord more than they earned.
• Jim Crow segregation in the South limited African-Americans’ access to skilled work and education; even in northern cities like Chicago and Detroit they faced housing discrimination and were sacked first when work slowed.
• Native Americans on reservations lived in extreme poverty — the 1928 Meriam Report described conditions as a national disgrace.
• Recent immigrants from southern and eastern Europe were funnelled into the lowest-paid factory jobs and faced the immigration restrictions of 1921 and 1924 (Lesson 5).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking specific groups to specific causes of exclusion, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples covering several groups.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one or two groups.
Emerging: Lists groups left out without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on American inequality in the 1920s: the collapse of farm prices, or the position of African-Americans? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the collapse of farm prices:
• Wheat fell from $2.50 to under $1 a bushel; cotton prices fell sharply too, hitting the largest single occupational group in 1920s America.
• Six million Americans were forced off their land — an enormous displacement that affected the entire countryside.
• Falling farm incomes pulled down rural communities of all races, making this a nationwide problem.

In support of the position of African-Americans:
• Jim Crow laws across the South locked African-Americans out of skilled work, decent schooling and voting, regardless of the national economy.
• Even northern industrial cities offered only segregated housing and the lowest-paid jobs.
• The double burden — sharecropping in the South and discrimination in the North — meant African-Americans faced inequality the wider country did not.

Judgement: The strongest answers note that the two intersected — African-American sharecroppers were hit twice over, by falling prices and by racial discrimination. A defensible verdict is that the collapse of farm prices was wider in scale, but the position of African-Americans was more fundamental because it would persist whether crops sold or not.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument weighing both factors, with precise detail and a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both factors but unevenly; judgement is asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Wall Street boom on different groups of Americans by 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• For wealthy investors and Wall Street brokers, rising share prices created enormous paper fortunes — speculators making 500%+ on companies like RCA.
• For middle-class clerks and small savers, buying on the margin made the market accessible — but their borrowed-up positions made them dangerously exposed.
• For ordinary depositors, banks investing their savings in the market meant they were exposed to a crash without ever buying a share.
• For farmers and sharecroppers, rising stock prices were irrelevant — their crop incomes fell across the decade and 6 million were forced off the land.
• For African-Americans and Native Americans, the boom was largely invisible: Jim Crow laws and reservation poverty kept them out of both the consumer society and the share-buying class.
• The effect overall was uneven prosperity at the top, hidden debt in the middle, and stagnation or decline at the bottom — setting up the unequal pain of the Crash in 1929 (Lesson 6).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation distinguishing effects across multiple named groups with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one or two groups.
Emerging: Identifies the boom without explaining its uneven effects.

lessons.title: Entertainment, Cinema and the Jazz Age
lessons.description: How Hollywood, radio and jazz reshaped what ordinary Americans did with their leisure time.
lessons.content_html:
A Country with Time on Its Hands

For the first time in American history, ordinary working people had spare cash and shorter working weeks. The average factory shift fell from 60 hours in 1900 to under 50 by 1929. Cars and electric trams meant Saturday afternoons could be spent at a stadium, a cinema or a dance hall instead of at home. The cultural Boom — cinema, radio, jazz, spectator sport — was inseparable from the economic one. It also marked a clear split with older, rural America: city pleasures shocked the small towns covered in Lesson 5.

Key Fact

By 1929 about 100 million cinema tickets were sold each week (in a country of 120 million), 10 million households owned a radio, and around 60,000 spectators packed Yankee Stadium to watch baseball. Mass leisure had become a major American industry.

Cinema and Hollywood

Cinema began the decade silent and ended it talking. Hollywood was already the centre of the world’s film industry by 1920 because of its sunshine, cheap labour and lax regulation. Studios — MGM, Paramount, Warner Brothers — built a star system around actors like Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford, Rudolph Valentino and Clara Bow (the ‘It Girl’). Tickets cost ten cents in the cheaper neighbourhood theatres. By 1929 there were over 23,000 cinemas in the USA — more than there were post offices.

In 1927 Warner Brothers released The Jazz Singer, the first feature with synchronised dialogue. The arrival of talkies was a technological revolution: silent stars who could not adapt (Valentino had died, but many others) saw their careers vanish, while new performers like Greta Garbo and James Cagney rose. By the early 1930s silent films had almost disappeared.

The big studios signed actors to long contracts, controlled which films they made and even chose what they wore in public. They also owned chains of cinemas, so a Paramount film almost always played in a Paramount cinema. The 1922 Hays Office, set up after a series of Hollywood scandals (the trial of Fatty Arbuckle, the murder of director William Desmond Taylor), introduced a code that censored on-screen drinking, nudity and crime — a sign that the Boom in popular culture was already being pushed back against by older America.

Radio and the Living-Room Boom

Radio arrived in homes faster than any previous technology. The first commercial broadcast went out in November 1920 from station KDKA in Pittsburgh. Within a decade nearly half of all American households owned a set, listening to news, music, comedy serials, baseball commentaries and political speeches. The first national network, NBC, launched in 1926. Advertisers bought slots during evening shows; political candidates began to record campaign messages. Radio shrank the country: a Texas farmer and a New York clerk could listen to the same programme on the same evening.

Jazz and the Soundtrack of the Decade

The 1920s are often called the Jazz Age, a phrase coined by F. Scott Fitzgerald. Jazz had grown out of the African-American communities of New Orleans and travelled north along the Mississippi to Chicago and on to New York’s Harlem with the Great Migration. Louis Armstrong (cornet and trumpet), Bessie Smith (blues vocals) and Duke Ellington (Cotton Club bandleader from 1927) became national stars. Dance crazes — the Charleston, the Black Bottom, the Lindy Hop — spread from speakeasies to college campuses to small-town high schools.

Jazz also exposed the racial divide. Black musicians played in clubs like the Cotton Club — but the audience was usually white-only, and many performers were paid less than the white-led bands. The Harlem Renaissance — a flowering of African-American writers including Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston — ran in parallel, building a cultural confidence that civil rights leaders would later draw on.

Spectator Sports and Heroes

Sport became its own industry. Babe Ruth’s 60-home-run season in 1927 made baseball a national obsession; Yankee Stadium opened in 1923 with capacity for 60,000. The boxer Jack Dempsey’s 1926 fight with Gene Tunney drew the first $2 million gate. The aviator Charles Lindbergh became the most famous American alive after his 1927 solo flight from New York to Paris — ticker-tape parades met him in every major city. Newspapers built sports sections to feed the appetite; radio carried the play-by-play.

Cinema, radio and sport all needed a new kind of newspaper to feed them. The 1920s saw the rise of the American tabloid: the New York Daily News, founded in 1919, hit a circulation of over a million by 1925; the New York Daily Mirror and the New York Evening Graphic followed. Tabloids printed sport photographs, gossip about Hollywood stars, salacious court reports and confession features. The 1927 Snyder–Gray murder trial — a Long Island housewife and her lover convicted of killing her husband — was covered like a sporting fixture, complete with a smuggled photograph of Snyder’s electrocution that filled the entire Daily News front page. The papers helped invent the modern celebrity: an athlete, film star or accused murderer whose face the public would recognise from the news-stand. Older Americans complained that the press was sensationalising violence and immorality; younger urban readers loved it.

Key Fact

Mass culture was an urban phenomenon. Cinemas, jazz clubs and stadiums clustered in the cities. Rural America — the small farming towns of the South and Midwest — saw cinema as immoral, jazz as primitive and the Charleston as obscene. The 1920s were the decade in which a city/country culture gap opened up that would still matter politically a hundred years later.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an Explain Effects question on 1920s popular culture, use the four industries (cinema, radio, jazz, sport) as a structure but always link them back to the wider Boom — rising wages and shorter hours funded them, and Hollywood’s star system mirrored the consumer economy described in Lesson 1. The strongest answers also note the city/country split — many of the same Americans who loved jazz and the Charleston in New York were the ones older rural Americans were trying to legislate against (Prohibition, immigration limits, the KKK revival in Lesson 5). Examiners reward links across the unit, not isolated description.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cinema (110 million tickets a week by 1929) and the arrival of talkies in 1927 turned Hollywood into a global cultural power.
  • Radio reached 10 million homes by 1929, creating the first truly national audience for news, sport and advertising.
  • Jazz, the Charleston and stars like Louis Armstrong shaped the ‘Jazz Age’, but mass culture was urban — deepening the rural/urban split that drives Lesson 5.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the spread of cinema and radio change American life in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• By 1929 about 100 million cinema tickets were sold every week in a country of 120 million — cinema-going became the standard weekend leisure activity.
• Hollywood’s star system created national celebrities (Chaplin, Pickford, Bow), and films set fashion and consumer aspirations across the country.
• The 1927 talkie revolution made acting careers depend on voice as much as appearance and gave audiences in small towns access to the same stars as New York.
• Radio reached 10 million homes by 1929 and the formation of NBC in 1926 created the first national broadcasting network — allowing a Texas farmer and a New York clerk to hear the same baseball commentary or political speech.
• Advertising on prime-time radio reinforced the consumer economy from Lesson 1 by reaching millions of households every night.
• Both industries deepened the urban/rural split: city Americans embraced them; many rural communities saw them as immoral.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking cinema and radio to specific changes in everyday life with precise figures.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one industry or to description.
Emerging: Identifies cinema or radio without explaining their effects.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the rise of spectator sport reflect the wider 1920s Boom?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Shorter working hours and higher wages gave Americans both the time and the disposable income to attend matches — Yankee Stadium opened in 1923 with capacity for 60,000.
• The motor industry (Lesson 1) carried fans to stadiums and tracks, while radio (this lesson) carried play-by-play to those who stayed at home.
• Babe Ruth’s 60-home-run season in 1927 made him a national hero on the same scale as Hollywood stars — sport produced celebrities of equal cultural weight.
• Boxing draws like the 1926 Dempsey vs Tunney fight produced the first $2 million gate, showing how sport had become a major commercial industry.
• Aviator Charles Lindbergh’s 1927 New York to Paris flight was treated like a sporting victory; ticker-tape parades celebrated him in every major city.
• These effects all rested on the same combination as the wider Boom: a consumer audience, mass media advertising and rising urban prosperity.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects linking sport to the wider Boom with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies sports stars without explaining how they reflected the Boom.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on American life in the 1920s: the rise of Hollywood, or the rise of radio? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of Hollywood:
• Cinema-going reached around 100 million tickets a week by 1929 — a near-universal weekly habit.
• The Hollywood star system shaped fashion, consumer aspirations and gender roles (the flapper image owes much to Clara Bow).
• The 1927 arrival of talkies showed how quickly Hollywood could reshape entertainment culture.
• Hollywood’s reach was global; American films exported the consumer society to Europe and Latin America.

In support of radio:
• Radio entered the home directly, reaching 10 million households by 1929 every evening of the week.
• NBC’s 1926 launch created the first national audience — political speeches and baseball games could now reach the whole country live.
• Radio carried adverts that drove the consumer economy described in Lesson 1.
• Radio was cheaper and more frequent than cinema, so its cumulative impact on daily routines may have been greater.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that radio had the deeper impact on day-to-day life because it was domestic and frequent, while Hollywood had the bigger weekly cultural impact because of its star system and global reach. The strongest answers note that the two reinforced each other — Hollywood films were promoted on radio, and stars appeared on radio shows.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of jazz and Hollywood on the divide between urban and rural America in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Jazz clubs, cinemas and stadiums clustered in cities like New York, Chicago and Los Angeles, where they became central to weekend leisure.
• Many rural Americans, especially in the South and Midwest, saw jazz as immoral and primitive — church groups campaigned against it.
• The Charleston, with its short skirts and energetic dancing, was condemned by older Americans as obscene; some small towns banned public performances.
• The 1922 Hays Office was created to police Hollywood’s on-screen alcohol, crime and nudity in response to small-town anger at the studios’ perceived immorality.
• These cultural anxieties fed into the political backlash described in Lesson 5 — Prohibition, the revived KKK and immigration restriction were partly attempts by older rural America to push back against the new urban culture.
• The result was a deepening cultural and political divide that would persist long after the Boom itself ended.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking 1920s popular culture to a deepening urban/rural divide with specific examples.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies urban culture without explaining the rural reaction.

lessons.title: The Position of Women: Flappers and Their Limits
lessons.description: How far the flapper image matched the everyday lives of women in 1920s America.
lessons.content_html:
An Image and a Reality

The 1920s gave America one of its most iconic images: the flapper — bobbed hair, short dress, cigarette in hand, dancing the Charleston in a Manhattan club. The flapper looked like proof that women had been liberated. Look more closely and the picture splits in two: a small, mainly urban, mainly young, mainly middle-class group whose lives genuinely changed; and a much larger group of rural, working-class, immigrant and African-American women whose daily realities barely shifted.

Key Fact

In 1920 the 19th Amendment gave women the right to vote in federal elections. Across the decade flappers also drove cars, went out unchaperoned, smoked and drank in public, wore knee-length dresses and danced the Charleston. These were genuinely new freedoms — but they were largely confined to young, urban, middle-class white women.

What Changed: The Flapper’s World

The 19th Amendment was the political symbol of the change but it had been a long fight: the suffrage movement led by figures like Carrie Chapman Catt had campaigned since the 1880s, and women’s war work in 1917-18 had shifted the politics. After 1920 women could vote in every state. Public opinion shifted: in 1923 the Equal Rights Amendment was first proposed in Congress (though never passed during the decade). Female participation in higher education climbed, and a small but growing minority of women entered the professions.

Wyoming had given women the vote as early as 1869 as a territory, and by 1918 fifteen states had followed. The First World War tipped the balance nationally. Around 25,000 American women had served as nurses near the front and tens of thousands more had taken factory jobs, made munitions, run farms or volunteered with the Red Cross while men were called up. President Wilson, who had opposed female suffrage in 1916, told Congress in 1918 that votes for women were ‘vital to the winning of the war’. The 19th Amendment passed Congress in 1919 and was ratified by Tennessee — the deciding state — in August 1920. By the November 1920 election about 8 million women voted for the first time, though African-American women in the South were still blocked by Jim Crow laws covered in Lesson 2.

Domestic life shifted for those who could afford it. Electricity reached around 70% of urban households by 1929 and about 25% of farms; refrigerators, vacuum cleaners and washing machines (almost all bought on hire purchase) cut hours of housework. Women had more leisure time and more disposable income, which the cosmetics industry, fashion magazines and Hollywood studios were eager to capture. Birth rates fell as more women used contraception; family size in the cities dropped from an average of around four children to closer to three across the decade.

Working Women

More American women worked outside the home than ever before — about 10.5 million by 1929, around 25% of the female adult population. But equality at work was distant. Women earned roughly half a male wage for the same job. They were concentrated in ‘women’s work’: secretarial work, teaching (especially of young children), nursing, telephone operating, retail. The new office economy of 1920s America — advertising agencies, banks, big city stores — created hundreds of thousands of typing and switchboard jobs that were marketed almost exclusively to young single women.

Many employers operated marriage bars — rules that forced women to resign on marriage. School boards across the country imposed them on female teachers. Bigger industrial employers preferred male breadwinners and would dismiss married women first in any downturn. So the white-collar boom in clerical work was largely a boom for unmarried women in their twenties; once they married, the door closed. Top professions — law, medicine, engineering, banking — remained overwhelmingly male: women were under 5% of US doctors and lawyers in 1929.

Women in Rural America

For the millions of women on America’s farms, the 1920s looked very different. Without electricity, washing meant heating water on a wood stove; without refrigeration, food preservation meant canning every summer. Rural birth rates remained much higher than urban ones: many farms still depended on family labour. A 1929 survey by the Department of Agriculture found that the average farm wife worked over 60 hours a week. The flapper image — with its knee-length dress, lipstick and cigarette — would have been unthinkable in most small towns: it was both unaffordable and morally condemned.

African-American and Immigrant Women

For African-American women in the South, voting rights granted by the 19th Amendment were undermined by Jim Crow restrictions covered in Lesson 2 (literacy tests, poll taxes, intimidation). They also faced economic exclusion: most worked as domestic servants or sharecroppers’ wives, with little access to clerical or factory jobs. Recent immigrants from Italy, Poland and the Russian Empire often combined factory work, piecework at home and large families — their lives more closely resembled pre-war working-class women than the flappers in nearby cinemas.

Key Fact

The flapper image is misleading as a picture of all women. Genuine 1920s gains — the vote, white-collar work, the cosmetics and fashion industries, lower urban birth rates — mainly benefited young, urban, white, middle-class women. Rural women, working-class women, African-Americans and recent immigrants saw far less change.

A Limited Liberation

The flapper was a real cultural figure, but she was a small one. Most 1920s American women were not flappers. The decade matters less because it liberated women than because it produced an idea of liberation that women in the 1960s feminist movement (Lesson 13) would later pick up, criticise and extend. The Boom narrowed the gap between what women could do and what they were allowed to do — but it did not close it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Period Essay on women in the 1920s, do not just describe flappers — argue. Examiner reports flag students who treat the flapper image as proof that all women were liberated. The strongest answers split women into groups (urban middle class, rural, working class, African-American, immigrant) and weigh the gains for each. A defensible judgement is that the 1920s changed the rhetoric and image of American womanhood faster than the daily reality. Where you can, link forward to Lesson 13 on the women’s movement to show importance over time.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 19th Amendment (1920) gave women the federal vote and the flapper image symbolised new public freedoms in fashion, dancing and behaviour.
  • By 1929 about 10.5 million women worked outside the home, but earned half a male wage, were concentrated in clerical and teaching jobs and faced marriage bars.
  • Rural women, working-class women, African-American women and recent immigrant women saw very little of the flapper’s liberation — the unit’s opportunity-and-inequality lens applies as much here as to wealth.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the flapper image in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Flappers wore short bobbed hair, knee-length dresses and visible make-up — a deliberate break with the long hair and ankle-length skirts of pre-war fashion.
• They drove cars, went out unchaperoned, smoked and drank in public, often in speakeasies, signalling new social freedoms.
• They danced the Charleston, the Black Bottom and the Lindy Hop — energetic dances that scandalised older Americans.
• They appeared in Hollywood films (Clara Bow, the ‘It Girl’) and in cosmetics and fashion adverts that helped spread the image across the country.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the position of women in American society change during the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The 19th Amendment (1920) gave women the right to vote in all federal elections, the political symbol of a long-running suffrage campaign.
• The flapper image normalised new public behaviours — cars, cigarettes, dancing, going out unchaperoned — for young urban middle-class women.
• About 10.5 million women worked outside the home by 1929 (~25% of adult women), with the white-collar economy creating hundreds of thousands of typing and switchboard jobs marketed to young single women.
• Domestic appliances bought on hire purchase — refrigerators, washing machines, vacuum cleaners — reduced the hours of unpaid housework, especially in cities with electricity.

• In 1923 the Equal Rights Amendment was first proposed in Congress, though it did not pass.

Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of women's work in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• About 10.5 million women worked outside the home by 1929, roughly a quarter of the adult female population.
• Women earned approximately half a male wage for similar work, so the gender pay gap remained large despite higher employment.
• They were concentrated in ‘women’s work’ — secretarial work, teaching, nursing, telephone operating, shop work — rather than in higher-paid industries.
• Many employers, especially in teaching and clerical work, operated ‘marriage bars’ that forced women to resign once they married.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the lives of rural women in the 1920s differ from the lives of urban flappers?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Only about 25% of American farms had electricity by 1929, compared with 70% of urban households — so rural women still washed by heating water on a stove and stored food by canning.
• A 1929 Department of Agriculture survey found the average farm wife worked over 60 hours a week, with little of the consumer-society relief that domestic appliances brought to cities.
• Rural birth rates remained higher because farms relied on family labour, so rural women had less reproductive freedom even though contraception was beginning to spread in cities.
• Religious and small-town moral codes condemned flapper fashions and the Charleston as immoral; few rural women could have appeared in public with bobbed hair and a knee-length dress without serious social cost.
• Cinema, jazz and radio (Lesson 3) reached cities first, so rural women had less access to the cultural mass-market that helped define the flapper image.
• The result was a near-invisible flapper presence in rural America, where most women’s lives looked closer to pre-war patterns than to the Manhattan nightclub image.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained contrast across multiple aspects of daily life with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one aspect.
Emerging: Identifies a difference without explaining its scale.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on the position of women in 1920s America: the 19th Amendment, or new patterns of work and consumer life? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the 19th Amendment:
• It removed a fundamental civic exclusion: women could now vote in every state and stand for office.
• It produced symbolic political change — the 1923 Equal Rights Amendment proposal was unthinkable a generation earlier.
• The political principle, once established, made later legal gains (e.g. 1972 ERA push, Lesson 13) possible.

In support of work and consumer life:
• 10.5 million women working outside the home by 1929 reshaped daily life and household income on a scale far broader than the political vote.
• Electric appliances bought on hire purchase cut housework hours and gave urban women genuine leisure time.
• The fashion, cosmetics and Hollywood industries built a public female cultural identity that mattered as much in practice as the right to vote.
• Falling birth rates and growing access to contraception in cities transformed family life.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that the 19th Amendment was politically more important in the long run, but in the daily lives of 1920s women, the changes in work and consumer life had more immediate impact — especially because the vote did not always lead to higher female political participation in the South. The strongest answers also note that for rural and African-American women, neither factor produced very much change.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both factors unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of marriage bars and the wage gap on the lives of working women in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Marriage bars across teaching and clerical work forced women to resign on marriage, so the white-collar boom benefited mainly unmarried women in their twenties.
• Once married, women lost access to professional jobs and depended on a husband’s wage; this entrenched the male-breadwinner family.
• The wage gap — women earned about half a male wage for similar work — meant working women contributed important household income but were rarely able to support themselves alone.
• During downturns, employers tended to dismiss married women first, treating their wages as supplementary, deepening insecurity for working-class families.
• Top professions remained over 95% male: women were under 5% of doctors and lawyers in 1929, despite the rising number of women in higher education.
• The cumulative effect was that 1920s women had more access to work than ever before but were locked out of the most secure and best-paid roles — a contradiction the women’s movement of the 1960s and 70s would target (Lesson 13).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects linking marriage bars and the wage gap to women’s economic position with precise detail.

lessons.title: A Divided Society: Prohibition, Crime, the Klan and the Red Scare
lessons.description: Prohibition gangsters, the revived Klan, immigration limits and the Sacco and Vanzetti case.
lessons.content_html:
A Country at War with Itself

The 1920s did not just bring jazz and assembly lines. It brought the most ambitious social-engineering experiment in American history (Prohibition), the largest white supremacist movement the country had ever seen (the revived Klan), the tightest immigration laws in its history, and a panic about communism that produced one of its most controversial trials. These were all responses by older, white, Protestant, rural America to the changes covered in Lessons 1–4. The Boom split the country.

Key Fact

Four divisions defined 1920s America: Prohibition (1920–33, the 18th Amendment), the revived Ku Klux Klan (membership reached around 4–5 million by 1925), immigration restriction (Emergency Quota Act 1921, Immigration Act 1924) and the Red Scare, which culminated in the Sacco and Vanzetti trial of 1921.

Prohibition

Prohibition began in January 1920 with the 18th Amendment and the enforcing Volstead Act. Campaigners — the Anti-Saloon League, the Women’s Christian Temperance Union, evangelical Protestant churches — argued that alcohol was destroying families, encouraging crime and ruining workers’ productivity. Their core support was rural, Protestant and white; they distrusted the saloons of the Catholic immigrant cities. Within months it was clear most Americans did not want to give up alcohol. The result was an enormous illegal economy.

Illegal bars known as speakeasies opened in every major city — New York alone had over 30,000 by 1929, more than the city had had legal saloons before Prohibition. Bootlegging stretched from rum-runners off the Florida coast to backyard stills in West Virginia. Federal Prohibition agents (only about 1,500 nationally) could not police a country that did not want to be policed.

Al Capone built a Chicago empire on bootleg alcohol, gambling and protection rackets. He bribed the mayor, the police chief and many federal agents; estimates put his gang’s 1927 income at around $60 million. Rival gangs fought over distribution — the St Valentine’s Day Massacre of 1929 saw Capone’s men gun down seven Bugs Moran gangsters. Federal agents could not catch Capone for murder; in 1931 he was finally jailed for tax evasion. He had, however, demonstrated that Prohibition had handed an entire industry to organised crime.

The Ku Klux Klan Revived

The original Klan had been crushed in the 1870s. A new Ku Klux Klan was launched in Georgia in 1915, inspired in part by the Hollywood film The Birth of a Nation. Through the early 1920s it grew into a mass movement, its membership peaking at perhaps 4–5 million by 1925. Its targets were not just African-Americans but also Catholics, Jews and recent immigrants — anyone who did not fit the WASP (White Anglo-Saxon Protestant) ideal. It dominated state politics in Indiana, Oregon and Colorado. Its hooded marches, cross-burnings and lynchings spread fear across the South and into the Midwest.

The Klan’s influence collapsed almost as fast as it grew. In 1925 D. C. Stephenson, the Grand Dragon of Indiana, was convicted of the rape and murder of a young woman, Madge Oberholtzer. The trial exposed the Klan’s violence and corruption, and membership halved in two years. By 1929 the Klan was a fraction of its 1925 size — though the prejudice that had powered it remained.

Immigration Restriction

For most of its history the USA had welcomed mass immigration. Between 1900 and 1914 around 13 million Europeans arrived. After the First World War, fear of revolution, the new Red Scare (below) and racism towards southern and eastern Europeans changed the politics. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 capped overall immigration at around 357,000 a year and set quotas favouring northern Europeans. The Immigration Act of 1924 went further: it cut overall immigration to 165,000 a year and pegged the quotas to the 1890 census — before most southern and eastern Europeans had arrived. Asian immigration was banned outright. The 1924 Act was the basis of US immigration policy for the next 41 years.

The Klan, Prohibition and the immigration Acts shared a base of supporters and a shared anxiety. By 1920 over half of all Americans lived in cities for the first time; the cities were full of southern and eastern Europeans, Catholics, Jews and African-Americans up from the South. The 1920 census made the change visible to anyone who read the figures. Older WASP (White Anglo-Saxon Protestant) America — rural, Protestant, north-western European in origin — saw its dominance slipping and reached for laws to reverse it. The 1924 Immigration Act was drafted by Albert Johnson, who openly cited ‘eugenic’ arguments about race; the Klan’s growth was strongest in midwestern states like Indiana whose populations had been shifting fastest; Prohibition aimed at the saloons of Catholic immigrant cities. Treat these as one connected backlash, not three separate stories — that is how examiners reward an answer.

The Red Scare and Sacco and Vanzetti

The 1917 Russian Revolution had terrified American business and government. The 1919 strike wave (over 4 million workers walked out, including the Boston police) and a series of anarchist letter bombs convinced Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer that communism was an immediate threat. The Red Scare peaked in the 1919–20 Palmer Raids: thousands were arrested, 556 immigrants were deported without trial. Civil-liberties campaigners protested, but the political climate had shifted decisively against the foreign-born and the political left.

In April 1920 a paymaster and a guard were shot dead in a robbery at a shoe factory in Massachusetts. Two Italian immigrants — Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti — were arrested. Both were known anarchists who had dodged the wartime draft. The evidence was thin and contradictory; the trial judge, Webster Thayer, openly described the men as ‘anarchist bastards’. They were convicted in 1921 and, after seven years of appeals, executed in August 1927. The case became internationally famous as a symbol of how the Red Scare and immigration prejudice could combine to deny justice. The spec names Sacco and Vanzetti precisely because their case shows the intersection of three of this lesson’s themes: communism panic, immigration restriction and ethnic prejudice.

Key Fact

The Sacco and Vanzetti case (1920–27) is named in the spec because it captures three forces in one trial: anti-communist panic (Red Scare), prejudice against Italian-Americans, and the wider 1920s push to restrict immigration. Examiners reward students who explain its significance in those terms, not just retell the story.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Significance question on Sacco and Vanzetti, do not just describe the trial. Explain why historians remember it: it links the Red Scare, immigration restriction and ethnic prejudice in a single event, and it became a symbol used by civil-liberties campaigners for decades. For a 12-mark Period Essay on the divisions of the 1920s, the strongest structure weighs Prohibition, the Klan, immigration limits and the Red Scare against each other. Avoid the common error of treating these as separate stories — they shared the same rural-Protestant-white-Anglo-Saxon backlash against the changes of Lessons 1–4.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prohibition (1920–33) tried to eliminate alcohol but produced speakeasies, bootlegging and organised-crime empires like Al Capone’s in Chicago.
  • The revived Ku Klux Klan reached 4–5 million members by 1925 before collapsing after the 1925 Stephenson scandal; immigration was sharply cut by the 1921 Emergency Quota Act and the 1924 Immigration Act.
  • The Red Scare and the Sacco and Vanzetti case (1920–27) showed how fear of communism, immigrant prejudice and biased justice combined in one of the decade’s most divisive episodes.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Prohibition in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Prohibition was introduced by the 18th Amendment in January 1920 and enforced by the Volstead Act, banning the manufacture, sale and transport of alcohol.
• Illegal bars known as speakeasies opened across the country — New York alone had over 30,000 by 1929, more than its legal saloons before Prohibition.
• Bootlegging stretched from rum-runners off the coast to backyard stills inland; only around 1,500 federal agents were employed to police the entire country.
• Organised crime gangs, most famously Al Capone’s in Chicago, controlled the supply of illegal alcohol and used violence and bribery to protect their operations.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did Prohibition fail to achieve its aims?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Speakeasies multiplied rather than disappeared — New York had more illegal bars in the late 1920s than it had had legal saloons in 1919.
• Bootlegging and home-distilling were widespread; rum-runners brought alcohol from Canada and the Caribbean, while moonshine stills supplied rural areas.
• Organised crime grew rich and powerful: Al Capone’s Chicago operation took an estimated $60 million a year in 1927 from bootleg alcohol, gambling and protection rackets.
• Public officials were corrupted on a massive scale; police, prosecutors and politicians took bribes from gangs in many cities.
• Violence rose — gang wars over distribution culminated in the 1929 St Valentine’s Day Massacre.
• Federal Prohibition agents (around 1,500 nationally) were too few to police a country whose drinkers no longer accepted the law — even Hoover’s 1929 inquiry, the Wickersham Commission, would later admit Prohibition was unenforceable.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects showing how Prohibition produced the opposite of its aims, with precise figures.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies a failure without explaining its cause.

• It targeted African-Americans, Catholics, Jews and recent immigrants, defining itself by the WASP (White Anglo-Saxon Protestant) ideal.
• It dominated state politics in Indiana, Oregon and Colorado in the early 1920s, electing governors and members of Congress.
• Its activities included hooded marches, cross-burnings and lynchings, often unpunished by local courts and police.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did immigration policy change in the USA in the 1920s?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Before the First World War the USA had welcomed mass immigration — around 13 million Europeans arrived between 1900 and 1914.
• The 1921 Emergency Quota Act capped immigration at around 357,000 a year and tied national quotas to 3% of the foreign-born of each nationality in the 1910 census.
• The 1924 Immigration Act cut the overall total to 165,000 and pegged quotas to the 1890 census — before most southern and eastern Europeans had arrived — almost eliminating Italian, Polish and Russian arrivals.
• Asian immigration was banned outright by the 1924 Act, building on earlier exclusionary laws.
• The pattern of arrivals shifted decisively away from southern and eastern Europe and from Asia, in line with WASP campaigners’ preferences.
• The 1924 Act became the basis of US immigration policy for the next 41 years, until the Hart–Celler Act of 1965.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation tracing the legal change and its effects on the pattern of immigration with precise dates.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description of one Act.
Emerging: Names the Acts without explaining their effects.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on dividing American society in the 1920s: Prohibition, or immigration restriction? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of Prohibition:
• It tried to remake everyday life for the entire country, dividing rural Protestant supporters from urban Catholic and immigrant opponents.
• It produced organised crime on a national scale, with Al Capone’s Chicago empire and the St Valentine’s Day Massacre.
• It corrupted police, courts and politicians, undermining trust in government.
• It lasted 13 years and was constantly contested in Congress.

In support of immigration restriction:
• The 1921 and 1924 Acts almost eliminated southern and eastern European arrivals and banned Asian immigration outright.
• The 1924 Act remained the basis of US immigration policy for 41 years, far longer than Prohibition.
• It was an explicit racial selection of who counted as American, with effects on community formation in cities for decades.
• It legalised the racial nationalism the Klan had been campaigning for, demonstrating how the cultural backlash captured federal policy.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that Prohibition was more visible at the time but immigration restriction had the deeper, longer-lasting effect on American society. The strongest answers also note that the two were connected — both had support from the same WASP rural-Protestant base.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparison with precise detail and a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Sacco and Vanzetti case for divisions in 1920s America.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The case combined three of the decade’s defining tensions in a single trial: fear of communism (Red Scare), prejudice against Italian-Americans, and the move towards immigration restriction.
• The 1921 conviction rested on thin and contradictory evidence; the trial judge, Webster Thayer, openly described the defendants as ‘anarchist bastards’, suggesting bias rather than impartiality.
• Their seven-year appeal and 1927 execution provoked international protests — rallies in Paris, London and Berlin showed how an American local trial had become a global symbol.
• Civil-liberties campaigners (including the new ACLU, founded 1920) used the case to argue that the Red Scare had eroded due process — an argument that long outlasted the trial.
• In 1977, fifty years after their execution, Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis issued a posthumous proclamation acknowledging the unfair trial.
• The case is named in the AQA spec because it concentrates the divisions of 1920s America in one event — a useful reference for any 8-mark or 12-mark question on the period.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation of significance covering links to multiple 1920s themes and importance over time.
Secure: Clear explanation of why the case mattered.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to retelling the story.
Emerging: Describes the trial without explaining its significance.
