lessons.title: From Wall Street Crash to Depression America
lessons.description: Why the market collapsed in 1929 and how the slump hit unemployed workers, farmers and businessmen.
lessons.content_html:
From Roaring Twenties to Bread Lines

In September 1929 the Dow Jones industrial average peaked at 381 points. By July 1932 it had fallen to 41 — an 89% collapse. Twelve million Americans were out of work; thousands of banks had closed; queues for free bread stretched around city blocks. The Wall Street Crash itself lasted only a few weeks, but the slump it triggered — the Great Depression — lasted into the 1940s. This lesson tracks how it began and what it meant for ordinary Americans.

Key Fact

Four main causes drove the slump: over-production by industry (factories making more than people could buy), under-consumption caused by 1920s inequality, speculation on the stock market (Lesson 2), and bank failures (around 9,000 US banks closed between 1930 and 1933).

The Wall Street Crash, October 1929

Share prices began to wobble in early September 1929 as economists like Roger Babson warned the market was overvalued. On Thursday 24 October — Black Thursday — nearly 13 million shares were sold and prices began to collapse. A consortium of bankers led by Richard Whitney intervened and steadied the market briefly, but on Tuesday 29 October — Black Tuesday — over 16 million shares were dumped and the market lost around $14 billion of value in a single day. Many speculators who had bought on the margin (Lesson 2) were ruined. Banks that had loaned them money lost their loans; banks that had invested customers’ deposits in the same shares lost those too.

A stock-market crash by itself need not crash the wider economy. What made 1929 different was the structure underneath. Roughly 5% of Americans had taken a third of national income (Lesson 2), so most households had little spare cash. Industry had been over-producing — factories were already making more cars and washing machines than the buying public could absorb. When share-buyers stopped spending, factories cut production and laid off workers; unemployed workers stopped buying; more factories cut production. Falling prices then trapped farmers further in debt.

Banks were the third multiplier. Around 9,000 US banks failed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out the savings of nine million depositors (deposit insurance did not yet exist). Each failure pulled small businesses down with it. The 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff (Lesson 7) added a fourth: by raising US import duties to record levels, it triggered retaliation that strangled what was left of international trade.

Unemployment and Hoovervilles

Unemployment rose from around 1.6 million (3% of the workforce) in 1929 to 12–13 million (25%) by 1932. In some industrial cities the figure was much worse: Toledo, Ohio reached 80% unemployment among union members. There was no federal unemployment benefit; relief was patchy and provided mainly by overstretched local charities and churches. Soup kitchens served free meals; the Salvation Army ran bread lines.

Evicted families built shanty towns of cardboard, packing crates and tin sheets in city parks and on waste ground. Bitter Americans named these settlements Hoovervilles in mockery of the president they blamed for their poverty. The largest, in St Louis, housed several thousand people. Newspapers used as blankets were called ‘Hoover blankets’; empty trouser pockets turned inside out were ‘Hoover flags’.

Farmers and the Dust Bowl

Farmers had already been struggling since 1921 (Lesson 2). The Crash made things worse: crop prices halved again, and the banks that foreclosed on farms collapsed before the farms could be sold. Then nature added a disaster of its own. From 1931 onwards, drought struck the southern Great Plains. Decades of intensive ploughing had stripped the topsoil’s natural cover; without rain, the soil turned to dust. Massive black storms — the largest, on 14 April 1935, was called Black Sunday — rolled across the prairies, swallowing whole towns. The disaster zone became known as the Dust Bowl.

Around 2.5 million people fled the southern Plains, many heading west to California. Mocked as ‘Okies’ whether or not they came from Oklahoma, they were channelled into low-paid migrant farm work. John Steinbeck’s 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath made their story famous. The Dust Bowl explains why farm distress in the early 1930s went far beyond falling prices.

Businessmen and the Bonus Army

The Depression hit owners and workers alike. Around 25,000 American businesses failed in 1932 alone. Industrial production fell by nearly half between 1929 and 1932. The men in suits selling apples on street corners — a famous Depression image — were often former clerks and shop managers, not panhandlers.

In summer 1932 around 17,000 unemployed First World War veterans — the Bonus Army — marched on Washington with their families to demand early payment of a service bonus due in 1945. They camped on the Anacostia Flats just across the Potomac from the Capitol, building a shanty town that resembled a Hooverville. On 28 July 1932 General Douglas MacArthur led federal troops — including Major George Patton with cavalry — with bayonets, tear gas and tanks to clear the camp. Two veterans were shot dead and an infant died of tear-gas exposure. Hoover had ordered MacArthur to clear only the buildings, not pursue the veterans across the river; MacArthur ignored the order and burned the entire encampment. Newsreels of US soldiers attacking US war veterans destroyed what remained of Hoover’s public reputation, four months before the November election (Lesson 7).

Key Fact

The Depression was not just a story about Wall Street. By 1932 unemployment was at 25%, around 9,000 banks had failed, 25,000 businesses had collapsed, 2.5 million had fled the Dust Bowl and the Bonus Army had been driven from Washington by federal troops. The country was looking for a new president.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question on the Wall Street Crash, do not stop at ‘people lost their savings’. Track the chain: speculators ruined → banks fail → depositors’ savings wiped out → small businesses lose access to credit → demand collapses → unemployment rises → Hoovervilles. The strongest answers also link forward to Lesson 7: Hoover’s response — rugged individualism, the Hawley–Smoot Tariff and the dispersal of the Bonus Army — turned an economic disaster into a political one. A common misconception examiners flag is that the Crash itself caused the Depression directly; the Crash was the trigger but the underlying causes (over-production, under-consumption, speculation, fragile banks) had been building all decade.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 (Black Thursday and Black Tuesday) wiped out billions in share value and ended the speculative boom.
  • The Crash triggered the Great Depression: 25% unemployment by 1932, around 9,000 bank failures, 25,000 business collapses and Hoovervilles in every major city.
  • Farmers fled the Dust Bowl as drought and over-ploughing destroyed the southern Plains; the Bonus Army’s 1932 dispersal sealed the political downfall of President Hoover.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• On Black Thursday, 24 October 1929, nearly 13 million shares were sold on the New York Stock Exchange as prices began to collapse.
• On Black Tuesday, 29 October 1929, over 16 million shares were dumped and the market lost around $14 billion of value in a single day.
• Speculators who had bought on the margin were ruined — brokers’ loans (Lesson 2) had to be repaid in full even though the shares used as collateral were now worthless.

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the Wall Street Crash trigger the wider Great Depression?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Speculators who had bought on the margin were ruined; their broker loans, which had to be repaid in full, then collapsed banks that had lent the money.
• Banks had also invested customers’ deposits in the same shares; when prices fell, around 9,000 US banks failed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out the savings of around nine million depositors who had never bought shares.
• Falling consumer demand turned the existing 1920s problem of over-production into mass lay-offs — industrial production fell by nearly half between 1929 and 1932.
• Unemployment rose from 1.6 million (3%) in 1929 to 12–13 million (25%) by 1932; without federal unemployment benefit, families relied on charity, soup kitchens and bread lines.
• Bank failures pulled small businesses down: around 25,000 American businesses collapsed in 1932 alone.
• The 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff (Lesson 7) added an external layer by triggering retaliation that strangled international trade and deepened the slump.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from financial panic through bank failures and unemployment to political collapse, with precise figures.

Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description of the Crash itself.
Emerging: Identifies the Crash as a cause without explaining how it spread.

• ‘Black Sunday’, 14 April 1935, saw a massive dust storm darken the sky from Texas to Chicago — one of around fourteen major storms that year.
• Around 2.5 million people fled the southern Plains, many heading to California, where they were derisively called ‘Okies’ whatever their home state.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the Great Depression affect ordinary Americans by 1932?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Unemployment reached 25% nationally and 80% in some industrial cities like Toledo; without federal unemployment benefit, families queued at soup kitchens and church bread lines.
• Evicted families built shanty towns of cardboard and packing crates — the ‘Hoovervilles’ named in bitter mockery of the president; the largest, in St Louis, housed thousands.
• Around 9,000 banks failed, wiping out the savings of nine million depositors who had no deposit insurance.
• Around 25,000 businesses collapsed in 1932 alone; suit-wearing former managers selling apples on street corners became a Depression image.
• In the southern Plains, the Dust Bowl forced 2.5 million people from their farms.
• In summer 1932 the Bonus Army of 17,000 First World War veterans was driven out of Washington by federal troops with bayonets and tear gas, after demanding early payment of a service bonus.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained explanation across multiple groups with precise figures and named events.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one group.
Emerging: Identifies hardship without explaining its scale.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact in deepening the Great Depression: the failure of around 9,000 American banks, or the collapse of farm prices and the Dust Bowl? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of bank failures:
• Around 9,000 banks failed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out the savings of around nine million depositors, since deposit insurance did not yet exist.
• Bank failures destroyed credit for small businesses; around 25,000 collapsed in 1932 alone.
• Without functioning banks, mortgages and farm loans could not be rolled over — foreclosures rose sharply.
• The political crisis of bank panics by early 1933 forced Roosevelt’s ‘bank holiday’ in his first week (Lesson 7+).

In support of farm prices and the Dust Bowl:
• Crop prices had been falling since 1921 (Lesson 2); the Crash and 1930s drought halved them again, locking sharecroppers in debt.
• 2.5 million Americans fled the Plains as Black Sunday and similar storms made farming impossible.
• Migration to California overwhelmed local labour markets, suppressing wages and creating long-term communities of displaced families.
• The Dust Bowl made the Depression visible, reshaping American political appetite for federal intervention through the New Deal.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that bank failures had the wider economic impact (because they froze credit nationwide and wiped out savings) but the Dust Bowl had the deeper cultural and political impact (because it symbolised the collapse of American life and motivated specific New Deal programmes). The strongest answers note that both factors fed each other — bank failures foreclosed Plains farms; Plains foreclosures destroyed local banks.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of unemployment and homelessness on American society between 1929 and 1932.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Unemployment rose from 1.6 million (3%) in 1929 to 12–13 million (25%) by 1932 — with peaks of 80% in some industrial cities.
• Without federal benefit, families relied on local charity, churches and soup kitchens; the Salvation Army ran bread lines in every major city.
• Hoovervilles — shanty towns of cardboard and packing crates — appeared in city parks and on waste ground; the largest in St Louis housed thousands.
• ‘Hoover blankets’ (newspapers) and ‘Hoover flags’ (empty pockets turned inside out) entered everyday speech, blaming the president for the slump.
• Confidence in the federal government collapsed: the 1932 Bonus Army episode showed unemployed war veterans being driven from Washington by their own army.
• The political effect was decisive: by November 1932 voters were ready for a fundamentally different presidency, opening the way for Roosevelt’s landslide (Lesson 7).

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from individual hardship to political collapse with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to description.
Emerging: Identifies hardship without explaining its political effects.

lessons.title: Hoover's Response and Roosevelt's 1932 Election
lessons.description: Why Hoover became so unpopular and how Roosevelt's New Deal pitch swept the 1932 election.
lessons.content_html:
Two Presidents, Two Visions

By the summer of 1932 around 25% of Americans were unemployed and shanty towns named after the president lined the cities. Hoover insisted that recovery would come through patience, voluntary effort and the natural workings of the market. Franklin D. Roosevelt, the Democratic governor of New York, promised ‘a new deal for the American people’. The election was a referendum on the role of the federal government — and it ended a generation of Republican dominance.

Key Fact

Hoover’s main responses to the Depression were the 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff (which made trade worse), the 1932 Reconstruction Finance Corporation (which lent to banks but came too late) and a continued belief in rugged individualism — that recovery should come through self-reliance rather than federal aid. None convinced enough voters in 1932.

Hoover’s Worldview: Rugged Individualism

Rugged individualism was not a slogan he invented during the slump — it was the philosophy he had built his career on. As Secretary of Commerce in the 1920s he had championed voluntary cooperation between business, charity and local government. As president from March 1929 he insisted that direct federal welfare would corrupt the American character and that ‘prosperity is just around the corner’. The longer the slump lasted, the more out of touch this looked.

Hoover did act — just less, slower and later than the crisis demanded. He pressed business leaders not to cut wages or lay workers off (most ignored him after 1930). He authorised some federal public works (the Hoover Dam, formerly Boulder Dam, was begun in 1931). He set up the President’s Emergency Committee for Employment to coordinate charity. But the scale was tiny next to the scale of the slump.

The Hawley–Smoot Tariff and Its Backfire

In June 1930 Hoover signed the Hawley–Smoot Tariff, raising US import duties on over 20,000 goods to record levels. The intention was to protect American factories and farms from foreign competition. The result was the opposite. Within two years 25 trading partners had retaliated with their own tariffs. World trade halved between 1929 and 1934. American farmers, who depended on exports, lost their overseas markets even as crop prices collapsed at home. Over 1,000 economists had begged Hoover not to sign the bill; he ignored them. By 1932 it was a textbook example of a policy that worsened the problem it was meant to solve.

In January 1932 Hoover finally accepted that markets would not self-correct and signed the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC) into law. The RFC made $2 billion of federal loans available to banks, railroads and large businesses. It was the most direct federal intervention in the economy in peacetime. But Hoover insisted the RFC must not lend to individuals, families or municipalities — he wanted to support institutions, not people. Critics called it ‘a millionaires’ dole’. The RFC was kept by Roosevelt and became one tool of the New Deal — but in 1932 it came too late to rescue Hoover’s presidency.

Why Hoover Became So Unpopular

Hoover’s unpopularity by 1932 was not just about policy — it was about tone. He was a quiet, formal man who hated public speaking. He insisted on dressing for dinner in the White House every evening even as bread lines grew outside. When the Bonus Army was dispersed in July 1932 (Lesson 6) by federal troops with tear gas and bayonets, the newsreels were devastating: a president attacking his own war veterans. The names attached to the misery — Hoovervilles, Hoover blankets, Hoover flags — turned an economic crisis into a personal verdict.

Roosevelt’s 1932 Campaign

Franklin D. Roosevelt — FDR — was a different kind of politician. He had been struck down by polio in 1921 and could not walk unaided, but built a public image of reassuring strength. He had served as Assistant Secretary of the Navy under Wilson and as Democratic governor of New York from 1929, where he had launched a state relief programme that became a model for federal action. His July 1932 Democratic Convention speech promised ‘a new deal for the American people’ — he flew to Chicago to deliver it in person, breaking the convention that the candidate stayed away.

Roosevelt did not run alone. His wife Eleanor Roosevelt had been a Democratic Party organiser since the early 1920s and travelled the country mobilising women voters — she would later become the most politically active First Lady to that date. Behind FDR sat the ‘Brain Trust’, a group of academics from Columbia University — Raymond Moley, Rexford Tugwell and Adolf Berle — who drafted policy papers and speeches throughout the 1932 campaign. Their thinking shaped the alphabet agencies of the early New Deal: federal banking regulation, public-works employment, agricultural price support and a relief programme for the unemployed. Hoover, by contrast, increasingly relied on a small inner circle that did not believe in federal welfare. The two campaigns were not just different in tone — they were different in the kind of advice each candidate sought.

Roosevelt did not yet have a fully worked-out plan in 1932. The New Deal would be improvised after he took office (Lesson 8 onwards). But his campaign offered three things Hoover could not: an explicit promise of federal action, an attack on banks and big business, and confidence in his own voice. He campaigned in 38 states by train, an exhausting routine designed to show he was physically capable of the presidency.

The November 1932 Result

Roosevelt won 472 electoral college votes to Hoover’s 59. He took 42 of the 48 states and 57% of the popular vote. The Democrats also won large majorities in both houses of Congress. The Republican grip on the federal government, unbroken since 1921, was decisively over. The four months between November 1932 and Roosevelt’s March 1933 inauguration were the longest of the slump — bank panics intensified as Americans waited — but the political verdict was clear.

Key Fact

Roosevelt won the 1932 election with 472 electoral college votes to Hoover’s 59 (57% of the popular vote). His New Deal pitch and broadcast skill, combined with Hoover’s rigid ‘rugged individualism’, gave him one of the largest landslides of the twentieth century. From March 1933, his fireside chats on radio would explain New Deal policy directly to households, transforming the way a president communicated with voters.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question on Hoover’s response to the Depression, do not just describe his policies — explain their effects. The Hawley–Smoot Tariff was meant to protect US industry but cut world trade by half; the RFC propped up large banks but refused aid to families; the dispersal of the Bonus Army was meant to restore order but destroyed his political reputation. For a 12-mark Period Essay comparing Hoover and Roosevelt, structure your answer around their philosophies (rugged individualism vs federal action) before evaluating particular policies. The strongest answers note that Roosevelt did not yet have a finished New Deal in 1932 — he won by promising action, not by promising specific policies.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hoover’s response to the Depression rested on rugged individualism, the 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff and the 1932 Reconstruction Finance Corporation — all of which fell short of the slump’s scale.
  • Hoovervilles, the Bonus Army dispersal and his cold public manner made Hoover a hate figure by 1932; voters were ready for a fundamentally different presidency.
  • Roosevelt’s 1932 landslide (472 electoral votes to 59, 42 states) and his promise of ‘a new deal for the American people’ opened the way for the New Deal era covered from Lesson 8 onwards.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Hoover's response to the Great Depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rugged individualism — Hoover insisted that Americans should overcome the slump through self-reliance, voluntary cooperation and local charity rather than federal welfare.
• The 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff raised US import duties on over 20,000 goods to record levels in an attempt to protect American factories and farms.
• The 1932 Reconstruction Finance Corporation made $2 billion of federal loans available to banks, railroads and large businesses to prevent further failures.
• Hoover authorised some public works such as the Hoover Dam (begun 1931) but refused direct federal aid to individuals.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did Hoover's policies fail to solve the Depression?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rugged individualism told Americans to rely on themselves and on charity, but private giving could not match the scale of the slump — soup kitchens were overwhelmed and Hoovervilles spread.
• The Hawley–Smoot Tariff (1930) was meant to protect US industry but provoked retaliation by 25 trading partners; world trade halved between 1929 and 1934, devastating American farm exports.
• The Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932) lent to banks and large businesses but Hoover refused to extend it to families or municipalities — critics called it ‘a millionaires’ dole’.
• Hoover’s federal public works (Hoover Dam) were tiny relative to the 12–13 million unemployed and could not stem mass joblessness.
• The dispersal of the Bonus Army in July 1932 by federal troops destroyed what remained of his moral authority.
• The cumulative effect was that the slump deepened on his watch and the political appetite shifted decisively towards federal intervention — opening the way for Roosevelt’s landslide.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects across multiple policies with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to one policy.
Emerging: Identifies a failure without explaining its cause.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Franklin D. Roosevelt's 1932 election campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Roosevelt promised ‘a new deal for the American people’ in his July 1932 Democratic Convention speech — the slogan that would define his presidency.
• He flew to Chicago to deliver his nomination acceptance in person, breaking the tradition that candidates stayed away from the convention — signalling activism.
• He campaigned in 38 states by train, an exhausting routine designed to show he was physically capable despite having had polio since 1921.
• His campaign attacked banks, big business and Hoover’s rugged individualism while promising explicit federal action; he avoided detailed plans, focusing on confidence and tone.

[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a basic identification, 2 for a developed feature]

practice_questions.text: In what ways did the dispersal of the Bonus Army in July 1932 damage Hoover's chances of re-election?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around 17,000 unemployed First World War veterans had marched on Washington and camped near the Capitol demanding early payment of a service bonus due in 1945.
• On 28 July 1932 General Douglas MacArthur led federal troops with bayonets, tear gas and tanks to clear the camp — against orders to be cautious.
• Two veterans were shot dead and an infant died of tear-gas exposure; the camp was burned to the ground.
• Newsreel footage of US soldiers attacking US war veterans circulated in cinemas across the country.
• The episode confirmed Hoover’s public image as cold and out of touch — reinforcing the message of Hoovervilles and Hoover blankets.
• It came just four months before the November election; Roosevelt used the contrast to position himself as the candidate of compassion and action, helping deliver his 472–59 electoral landslide.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from a single event to the political verdict, with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to retelling the event.
Emerging: Identifies the dispersal without explaining its political effect.

practice_questions.text: Which had more impact on Hoover's defeat in 1932: his economic policies, or his public image? Explain your answer with reference to both.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh both factors and reach a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of his economic policies:
• The Hawley–Smoot Tariff (1930) cut world trade in half by 1934 and was condemned in advance by over 1,000 economists.
• The RFC (1932) lent to banks but refused individuals or local government, leaving most Americans untouched by federal aid.
• Rugged individualism rested on the belief that voluntary effort would suffice; with 12–13 million unemployed, voters had stopped believing it.
• His policies failed to halt 9,000 bank failures, 25,000 business collapses and 25% unemployment.

In support of his public image:
• Hoover refused to invite reporters into the White House and disliked public speaking, leaving him unable to defend his record on radio.
• Hoovervilles, Hoover blankets and Hoover flags personalised the Depression as his fault.
• His decision to dress for dinner in the White House every night while bread lines grew outside became a symbol of his detachment.
• The dispersal of the Bonus Army by federal troops in July 1932 confirmed an image of cold authority.

Judgement: A defensible verdict is that the policies caused the slump to deepen, but it was Hoover’s public image — especially after the Bonus Army — that delivered the scale of his defeat. The strongest answers note that the two reinforced each other: had Hoover communicated like Roosevelt, he might have softened the political damage from his economic record; had his record been better, his cold manner might have been forgiven.

[12 marks]
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with precise detail and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear comparison; reaches a judgement.
Developing: Discusses both unevenly; judgement asserted not substantiated.
Emerging: Lists features of each without comparing them.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Roosevelt's victory in the 1932 presidential election on the federal government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Roosevelt won 472 electoral votes to Hoover’s 59 and 42 of the 48 states — one of the largest landslides of the twentieth century.
• The Democrats also won large majorities in both houses of Congress, ending the Republican federal dominance that had run since 1921.
• The mandate gave Roosevelt the political space to launch the New Deal at speed once he was inaugurated in March 1933 — the ‘Hundred Days’ (Lesson 8) saw 15 major laws passed.
• Confidence in federal government rose during the four-month inter-regnum, even as bank panics deepened, because voters expected change.
• Roosevelt’s fireside chats from 1933 onwards transformed the relationship between president and public — explaining policy directly through radio.
• The 1932 election also realigned American politics for a generation — the New Deal coalition (urban workers, southern Democrats, African-Americans, organised labour) would dominate elections until the late 1960s.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained chain of effects from electoral landslide to long-term political realignment with precise detail.
Secure: Clear explanation of effects with relevant examples.
Developing: Some explanation, weighted to the result itself.
Emerging: Identifies that Roosevelt won without explaining the consequences.

lessons.title: The First New Deal: Hundred Days and the Alphabet Agencies
lessons.description: Roosevelt's first hundred days, the alphabet agencies and the rebuilding of confidence in 1933.
lessons.content_html:
A Country in Free Fall

When Franklin Roosevelt was sworn in on 4 March 1933, around 13 million Americans were unemployed — about a quarter of the workforce. Thousands of banks had collapsed since 1929, wiping out the savings of millions of depositors. Industrial production had halved. Hoover’s belief in ‘rugged individualism’ and minimal federal action had been overtaken by events. Roosevelt’s inaugural address declared, “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” and promised ‘action, and action now’. The next three months — the Hundred Days — produced the most active legislative period in American peacetime history.

Key Fact

Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933 with around 13 million Americans unemployed and a banking system in collapse. In his first hundred days Congress passed 15 major laws and created the alphabet agencies that defined the First New Deal.

Banking First: The Emergency Banking Act

Roosevelt’s first move was to stop the bleeding. On 6 March he declared a four-day ‘bank holiday’ and closed every bank in the country. On 9 March Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act in just eight hours. Treasury inspectors examined the books of every bank and reopened only those judged sound. On 12 March Roosevelt gave the first of his famous radio ‘fireside chats’ explaining what had been done in plain language. When banks reopened the following Monday, deposits flooded back in. Within a fortnight roughly $1 billion of cash had been redeposited. The panic was over.

In June 1933 the Glass-Steagall Act went further: it created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) which insured personal deposits up to $5,000 and separated commercial from investment banking. Together these measures restored confidence that money put in a bank would still be there in the morning — the foundation on which everything else depended.

The Alphabet Agencies

Confidence restored, Roosevelt then attacked unemployment. Congress created a flurry of new federal agencies, each known by its initials. Together they became the alphabet agencies.

The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), created in March 1933, gave young unmarried men aged 18–25 work in national forests, parks and on flood-control schemes. Recruits earned $30 a month, of which $25 was sent home to their families. Around 2.5 million young men passed through the CCC by 1942, planting roughly three billion trees and building 800 state parks. It was the most popular New Deal agency and became a symbol of recovery on the ground.

Farmers were saved by the Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA) of May 1933, which paid farmers to reduce production, lifted prices and refinanced farm mortgages. Some six million pigs were slaughtered to cut surpluses — controversial at a time when families were going hungry, but farm income rose by around 50% within two years. The Federal Emergency Relief Administration (FERA), led by Roosevelt’s adviser Harry Hopkins, distributed $500 million in direct grants to states for poor relief — a federal commitment to relief that had no precedent.

The TVA, NRA and PWA

The most ambitious project was the Tennessee Valley Authority. The Tennessee Valley covered seven southern states and was one of the poorest regions in America: soil exhausted by cotton farming, no electricity, regular flooding. The TVA built 20 dams, brought electricity to over half the valley’s homes by 1940, controlled floods and replanted forests. It was federal economic planning on a scale critics called socialist — and a transformation supporters called miraculous.

The National Recovery Administration (NRA), launched in June 1933, set codes of fair competition for industry covering wages, hours and prices. Businesses that signed up displayed the NRA’s blue eagle symbol. Roughly 2.5 million employers signed. The Public Works Administration (PWA), with a $3.3 billion budget, funded large infrastructure projects — the Hoover Dam, the Lincoln Tunnel, the Triborough Bridge in New York, schools, hospitals and aircraft carriers. Together NRA and PWA aimed to lift wages, employ men on big projects and prime the pump of the wider economy.

CCC — relief: jobs for young unmarried men in conservation, $30 a month with $25 sent home. AAA — recovery: paid farmers to cut production to lift prices. CCC and AAA were the headline relief and farm measures. TVA — reform: federal regional planning, dams and hydroelectricity for the Tennessee Valley. NRA — recovery: industry codes on wages, hours and prices, blue eagle symbol. PWA — recovery: $3.3 billion for large public works. FERA — relief: federal grants to states for direct poor relief. The agencies are commonly grouped under Roosevelt’s ‘three Rs’: Relief, Recovery and Reform.

A New Federal Government

The Hundred Days did more than create agencies. They redrew the relationship between Washington and ordinary American life. For the first time in peacetime, the federal government employed people directly, regulated wages and prices, paid farmers, insured deposits and built infrastructure on a national scale. Roosevelt’s fireside chats — intimate radio addresses delivered in clear language — turned the presidency into a daily presence in 60 million homes that owned a radio. By the end of June 1933, unemployment had fallen modestly and confidence had risen sharply. The First New Deal had not ended the Depression. It had, however, prevented collapse and given Americans the sense that someone was in charge.

Key Fact

The First New Deal is often summarised by Roosevelt’s ‘three Rs’: Relief (FERA, CCC), Recovery (AAA, NRA, PWA) and Reform (TVA, FDIC under Glass-Steagall). It did not end the Depression, but stopped the collapse and rebuilt confidence.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Explain Effects question, do not list agencies. Pick two or three effects (banking confidence, farm income, mass relief employment, federal scope) and develop each with a specific example and figure. Examiner reports flag students who write ‘agency soup’ — long lists of initials with no causal link. For 12-mark Period Essays, the misconception to avoid is that the New Deal ended the Depression. The First New Deal cushioned suffering and rebuilt confidence; only the war economy from 1941 returned the USA to full employment.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Hundred Days (March–June 1933) produced 15 major laws including the Emergency Banking Act, AAA, CCC, TVA, NRA, PWA and FERA.
  • Roosevelt’s ‘three Rs’ — Relief, Recovery, Reform — describe what the alphabet agencies were trying to do, not just what they were called.
  • The First New Deal stopped the collapse and rebuilt confidence but did not end the Depression; full recovery came only with war production from 1941.

Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the alphabet agencies as a wasteful expansion of federal power that bypassed Congress and undermined private enterprise.
• Interpretation B presents the TVA as a transformation that brought tangible improvements — electricity, flood control, jobs — to one of the poorest regions in America.
• Main difference: A frames the New Deal as overreach by Washington; B frames it as targeted help that local communities welcomed.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1933 Republican editorial) and Interpretation B (a 1934 article by a Tennessee Valley farmer) give different views about the First New Deal.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the editorial spoke to readers worried about federal power and big government; the farmer’s article spoke to neighbours who had benefited directly from TVA dams.
• They use different evidence — the editorial cites federal spending and constitutional concerns; the farmer cites electricity reaching his farm and flood damage prevented.
• They were produced from different positions — an urban Republican commentator opposed to Roosevelt versus a rural beneficiary in a poor region transformed by the TVA.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘Roosevelt’s first hundred days saved American capitalism from collapse.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the impact of the First New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Emergency Banking Act of 9 March 1933 stopped a banking collapse: $1 billion of deposits flooded back within a fortnight after the four-day bank holiday and Treasury inspections.
• Convincing because Glass-Steagall and the FDIC restored confidence that personal savings up to $5,000 were safe.
• Convincing because the alphabet agencies (CCC, FERA, AAA, NRA, PWA, TVA) employed millions and lifted farm income by around 50% in two years.
• Less convincing because unemployment remained high — around 11 million still out of work in 1934 — and full recovery only came with war production from 1941.
• Less convincing because the Supreme Court later struck down the NRA (1935) and AAA (1936) as unconstitutional, exposing structural weaknesses.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing in stopping the collapse and rebuilding confidence; less convincing as an explanation of full economic recovery.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Emergency Banking Act of March 1933 on the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stopped the banking panic — the four-day bank holiday closed every bank for inspection; only those judged solvent reopened on 13 March, and around $1 billion of cash flooded back into deposits within a fortnight.
• Restored confidence through Roosevelt’s first fireside chat on 12 March, which explained the rescue in plain language to 60 million radio homes — reframing the federal government as protector rather than spectator.
• Created the foundation for further reform — the June 1933 Glass-Steagall Act built on the success by establishing the FDIC, which insured deposits up to $5,000 and separated commercial from investment banking.
• Saved roughly 5,000 sound banks by allowing supervised reopening, and permanently reduced the rate of bank failures — the lifeblood without which alphabet-agency spending could not have circulated through the economy.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why Roosevelt’s First New Deal had a major impact on the United States in 1933–34.
You may consider:
• the banking and farm rescue measures
• the alphabet agencies and federal employment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Banking rescue: the Emergency Banking Act (9 March 1933) closed banks for inspection; reopening triggered $1 billion of redeposits; Glass-Steagall (June 1933) created the FDIC insuring savings up to $5,000.
• Farm rescue: the AAA (May 1933) paid farmers to cut production; six million pigs slaughtered; farm income rose around 50% within two years.
• Mass relief: FERA distributed $500 million through Harry Hopkins; CCC employed 2.5 million young men by 1942 at $30/month; CCC built 800 state parks and planted three billion trees.
• Industrial recovery: NRA codes on wages, hours and prices; blue eagle symbol; 2.5 million employers signed up. PWA $3.3 billion built the Hoover Dam, Lincoln Tunnel, Triborough Bridge.
• Regional reform: TVA built 20 dams in seven southern states, brought electricity to over half the valley by 1940 and controlled flooding.
• Communication: fireside chats turned the presidency into a daily presence in 60 million radio homes.
• Limits: 11 million still unemployed in 1934; the New Deal cushioned but did not end the Depression; the Supreme Court later struck down NRA (1935) and AAA (1936).
• Conclusion: the First New Deal’s major impact was political and psychological as well as economic — it stopped the collapse, rebuilt confidence and redrew the role of the federal government in American life, even though full recovery would have to wait for the war.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The CCC enrolled young unmarried men aged 18–25 in conservation work in national forests, parks and on flood-control schemes. Around 2.5 million young men passed through it by 1942.
• Recruits were paid $30 a month, of which $25 was sent home to their families — combining direct relief for young men with cash transfers to households still suffering from unemployment.
• The CCC planted roughly three billion trees, built 800 state parks and constructed thousands of miles of trails — visible improvements to the American landscape that built support for the New Deal.
• It was administered jointly by the Departments of Labor, Interior and Agriculture and the Army, which ran the camps in military style — controversial to some but giving recruits structure and skills.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

lessons.title: Effectiveness, Opposition and the Second New Deal
lessons.description: Who the New Deal helped and missed, the Court and radical opposition, and the 1935 Second New Deal.
lessons.content_html:
A New Deal — for Whom?

By 1934 the First New Deal had stopped the collapse, but the Depression had not ended. Around 11 million Americans were still unemployed. As Roosevelt’s programmes settled into operation, the question shifted from ‘will it work?’ to ‘who is it working for?’. The honest answer is uneven: the New Deal helped some groups powerfully and largely failed others. It also drew loud opposition from three different directions — the Supreme Court, congressional Republicans, and radical critics who argued Roosevelt had not gone nearly far enough. The political pressure forced the ‘Second New Deal’ of 1935.

Key Fact

The New Deal helped industrial workers, farmers and the elderly — through union recognition, AAA payments and Social Security pensions. It largely failed African-Americans, Mexican-Americans and Native Americans. Inequality remained a defining feature of recovery.

Who Benefited Most

Industrial workers were among the biggest winners. The 1935 Wagner Act guaranteed the right to join a trade union and bargain collectively. Union membership doubled from around 3.6 million in 1935 to 8.7 million by 1940. Farmers saw their incomes rise by around 50% in two years thanks to AAA payments. Older Americans gained Social Security pensions. Around 8.5 million workers found employment through the Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935) building schools, post offices and roads. White women benefited from FERA and WPA jobs, even where pay was lower than men’s. Eleanor Roosevelt actively lobbied her husband to direct New Deal money towards women, miners and the rural poor.

Who Was Left Out

African-Americans gained much less. The AAA paid landowners to take fields out of production, but the cuts hit black sharecroppers and tenant farmers hardest — many were evicted. NRA codes set lower wages for southern workers, where most black Americans lived. Roosevelt refused to back a federal anti-lynching bill because he needed southern Democratic votes in Congress for the rest of his programme. CCC camps were segregated. Some 200,000 black Americans did join the CCC, and Roosevelt’s informal ‘Black Cabinet’ of African-American advisers (including Mary McLeod Bethune) gave the New Deal a moral language on race that earlier presidents had refused. But on the ground, the colour line held.

Mexican-Americans were excluded from many programmes and roughly 500,000 were ‘repatriated’ — in many cases deported — during the 1930s. Native Americans gained more under the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act, which ended the policy of forced assimilation and restored some tribal land rights, but rural poverty persisted. Domestic and agricultural workers (the bulk of black and Hispanic women’s employment) were excluded from Social Security entirely.

Women’s gains were real but limited. Frances Perkins became the first female Cabinet member as Secretary of Labor. Eleanor Roosevelt held weekly press conferences open only to women reporters and lobbied for women’s relief. Around 8,500 women were enrolled in a women’s version of the CCC. But NRA codes often set female wages below men’s, the CCC excluded married women, and the breadwinner ideology was reinforced rather than challenged. The Depression pushed many married women out of paid work to free up jobs for unemployed men.

Opposition from the Supreme Court

The most damaging early opposition came from the Supreme Court. In Schechter v. United States (May 1935) the Court unanimously struck down the NRA as an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power and federal interference with intra-state commerce. In United States v. Butler (January 1936) the Court struck down the AAA on similar grounds. Roosevelt was furious. In 1937 he proposed his ‘court-packing plan’: legislation that would let him appoint up to six new justices to outvote the conservative bloc. Even Democrats called it dictatorial. Congress rejected the plan, but the Court began to uphold New Deal legislation more sympathetically (the so-called ‘switch in time that saved nine’).

Republican and Radical Opposition

Republicans attacked the New Deal as an attack on individual liberty and a step towards socialism. Critics like Wendell Willkie warned that federal spending was unsustainable and that programmes like the TVA undermined private utility companies. The 1936 Republican candidate Alf Landon was crushed in a landslide — Roosevelt won 46 of 48 states — but Republican opposition would harden through Roosevelt’s second term.

More dangerous, politically, were radical critics who argued that the New Deal had not gone far enough. Senator Huey Long of Louisiana proposed his ‘Share Our Wealth’ programme — confiscate the great fortunes and give every family $5,000 and a guaranteed income. Father Charles Coughlin used his weekly radio broadcasts (40 million listeners at peak) to demand bank nationalisation and silver-backed currency, sliding into open antisemitism by 1936. Dr Francis Townsend proposed a $200-a-month pension for everyone over 60 to be spent within 30 days. Long was assassinated in September 1935; Coughlin was eventually silenced by the Catholic hierarchy. But by 1935 the three radical critics had together convinced Roosevelt that he needed bolder reforms or risked losing the centre to a populist challenger.

Even at the worst of the Depression, around 60 million Americans went to the cinema each week. Hollywood produced screwball comedies and gangster films offering escape; Walt Disney’s Snow White (1937) was the highest-grossing film of the decade. Radio reached 28 million households by 1939; Roosevelt’s fireside chats and Coughlin’s broadcasts both depended on the medium. Federal Project Number One under the WPA paid 40,000 unemployed artists, writers, photographers and musicians — producing post office murals, the Federal Theatre Project and Dorothea Lange’s photographs of migrant workers. Popular culture both distracted from suffering and documented it.

The Second New Deal, 1935

The political pressure produced a sharper, more redistributive package in 1935. The Wagner Act guaranteed union rights, partly answering radical demands for worker power. The Social Security Act of August 1935 created federal pensions for the elderly, unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children — the first national welfare system in American history, though limited (it excluded domestic and agricultural workers). The WPA gave employment to 8.5 million workers between 1935 and 1943. A ‘wealth tax’ raised top federal income tax rates to 75% on the highest earners. Roosevelt’s contribution as president now included not just the Hundred Days but a sustained ability to move with political pressure rather than be broken by it.

Key Fact

The Second New Deal of 1935 included the Wagner Act (union rights), the Social Security Act (pensions, unemployment insurance, aid to dependent children) and the WPA (work for 8.5 million). It was driven by Court strikes, radical pressure and the 1936 election — and was more redistributive than the First New Deal.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Evaluate questions on New Deal effectiveness, the strongest answers handle the ‘helped some, failed others’ tension explicitly — do not write the New Deal off as a failure, but do not pretend it ended inequality either. Examiner reports flag the misconception that the New Deal ended the Depression: it did not, but that does not make it a failure. For 12-mark Period Essays comparing Roosevelt’s contribution against structural factors, weigh his political skill (fireside chats, the 1936 landslide) against the Court rulings, the radicals and the eventual war economy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The New Deal helped industrial workers, farmers and the elderly significantly; African-Americans, Mexican-Americans and domestic workers were largely left out.
  • Opposition came from three directions: the Supreme Court (striking down NRA in 1935 and AAA in 1936), congressional Republicans, and radical critics — Huey Long, Father Coughlin and Dr Townsend — who said Roosevelt had not gone far enough.
  • The Second New Deal of 1935 (Wagner Act, Social Security Act, WPA) was Roosevelt’s response to that pressure — more redistributive and more focused on workers and the poor than the First.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1935 speech by Senator Huey Long arguing the New Deal had failed to help working people enough) and Interpretation B (a 1936 Democratic Party campaign leaflet praising Social Security and the Wagner Act). What is the main difference between these views about the New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the New Deal as inadequate — the rich kept their fortunes and ordinary Americans had not been lifted out of hardship.
• Interpretation B presents the New Deal as a transformation — pensions, unemployment insurance and union rights for the first time in American history.
• Main difference: A frames the New Deal as a missed chance for radical redistribution; B frames it as a historic achievement that helped working Americans.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1935 Huey Long speech) and Interpretation B (a 1936 Democratic Party campaign leaflet) give different views about the New Deal.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — Long’s speech aimed to recruit support for his Share Our Wealth movement and a possible 1936 presidential challenge; the campaign leaflet aimed to re-elect Roosevelt.
• They use different evidence — Long cites the persistence of great private fortunes; the leaflet cites the Wagner Act and Social Security as concrete reforms.
• They were produced from different political positions — a populist senator to the left of Roosevelt versus the official Democratic campaign defending the President’s record.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘The New Deal failed African-Americans more than it helped them.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the experience of African-Americans under the New Deal?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because AAA payments to landowners encouraged the eviction of black sharecroppers and tenant farmers across the South.
• Convincing because NRA codes set lower wages for southern workers, where most black Americans lived; CCC camps were segregated; and Roosevelt refused to back a federal anti-lynching bill to keep southern Democratic votes.
• Convincing because domestic and agricultural workers, the bulk of black female employment, were excluded from Social Security.
• Less convincing because around 200,000 black Americans found CCC work; Roosevelt’s informal ‘Black Cabinet’ (including Mary McLeod Bethune) gave the federal government a moral language on race that earlier presidents had refused.
• Less convincing because federal relief and WPA employment did reach urban black communities, especially in northern cities — the 1936 black vote shifted decisively to the Democrats.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing on rural and structural failures; partially overstated on the symbolic and federal-employment gains.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Supreme Court rulings against the New Deal between 1935 and 1936.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Schechter v. United States (May 1935) struck down the NRA as unconstitutional, ending the system of industry codes on wages, hours and prices, and forcing Roosevelt to find new constitutional foundations for federal action.
• United States v. Butler (January 1936) struck down the original AAA — the federal payment system to farmers had to be rebuilt under different legal authority via the 1938 second AAA.
• The rulings provoked Roosevelt’s 1937 court-packing plan to add up to six new justices, which was rejected by Congress and damaged his political authority during his second term.
• In response to the rulings, Roosevelt and Congress designed the 1935 Wagner Act and Social Security Act with stronger constitutional foundations — making the Second New Deal more focused on workers’ rights and federal taxation than direct industry regulation.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why Roosevelt launched a Second New Deal in 1935.
You may consider:
• Supreme Court strikes against the First New Deal
• pressure from radical critics such as Huey Long, Father Coughlin and Dr Townsend.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Court strikes: Schechter (May 1935) struck down the NRA; the AAA was vulnerable; Roosevelt needed reforms with safer constitutional foundations.
• Persistent unemployment: around 11 million still out of work in 1934; the First New Deal had stopped collapse but not delivered full recovery.
• Huey Long: Senator from Louisiana, ‘Share Our Wealth’ movement, $5,000 per family promise; threatened a 1936 third-party run before his assassination in September 1935.
• Father Coughlin: weekly radio broadcasts to 40 million listeners demanding bank nationalisation and silver-backed currency.
• Dr Townsend: $200-a-month pension proposal for the over-60s, with strong support among the elderly.
• 1936 election approaching: Roosevelt needed a sharper offer to working-class voters and the elderly.
• Result: Wagner Act (union rights); Social Security Act (pensions, unemployment insurance, aid to dependent children); WPA (8.5 million workers employed); wealth tax raising top rates to 75%.
• Outcome: Roosevelt won 46 of 48 states in 1936.
• Conclusion: the Second New Deal was Roosevelt’s response to a pincer of judicial blockage and populist pressure — the Court forced a constitutional rebuild and the radicals forced a redistributive turn.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Social Security Act of 1935.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It established federal pensions for retired Americans aged over 65, funded by payroll taxes on workers and employers — the first national old-age pension system in American history.
• It introduced unemployment insurance jointly run by the federal government and the states, providing a temporary income to workers who lost their jobs.
• It included aid to dependent children for poor families, particularly widows and abandoned mothers raising children alone.
• It excluded domestic and agricultural workers — meaning many African-American and Mexican-American women, and farm labourers, were not covered.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]

lessons.title: The Second World War and American Recovery
lessons.description: How war production, Lend Lease and home-front mobilisation ended the Depression in the 1940s.
lessons.content_html:
The War That Ended the Depression

In 1940 around 8 million Americans were still out of work and the Depression was in its eleventh year. By 1944 unemployment had effectively disappeared and the United States was producing roughly half of all the world’s manufactured goods. The Second World War achieved what the New Deal could not. Federal spending rose from $9 billion in 1939 to $98 billion by 1944. Forty-million Americans were drawn into uniform or war work between 1941 and 1945. The conflict also reshaped American society at home: black families moved north and west by the million, women entered industries previously closed to them, and the federal government became a permanent presence in everyday life.

Key Fact

Around 8 million Americans were still unemployed in 1940. The war economy from 1941 returned the USA to full employment by 1944. The Second World War — not the New Deal — ended the Great Depression.

Lend Lease and the Path to War

The Neutrality Acts of 1935–37 had committed the USA to staying out of European wars. But by 1940 Britain stood alone against Nazi Germany and could no longer pay cash for American supplies. Roosevelt persuaded Congress to pass the Lend-Lease Act in March 1941, allowing the USA to ‘lend or lease’ weapons, food and oil to Britain and later to the Soviet Union without immediate payment. By 1945 around $50 billion of supplies had been shipped — about $32 billion to Britain, $11 billion to the USSR. Roosevelt described the policy as lending a neighbour your hose if their house was on fire. American factories began to fill with orders even before Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 ended the debate over neutrality. Within four days the United States was at war with Japan, Germany and Italy. The transformation of the American economy — long under way thanks to Lend Lease — now accelerated dramatically.

The Arsenal of Democracy

War production figures dwarf anything the New Deal had attempted. Between 1941 and 1945 the United States built around 297,000 aircraft, 86,000 tanks, 8,800 warships and 41 billion rounds of small-arms ammunition. The Ford Willow Run plant in Michigan rolled out a B-24 bomber every 63 minutes at peak. Henry Kaiser’s shipyards launched a Liberty cargo ship in just 4–5 days using assembly-line techniques borrowed from car manufacturing. Roosevelt called the United States ‘the arsenal of democracy’ in a December 1940 fireside chat — by 1945 the description was understatement.

Federal spending pumped this expansion. The War Production Board (1942) directed materials and labour. Wages rose by around 65% during the war as factories competed for workers. Personal income tax was extended to most workers for the first time, and the federal government employed around 4 million people directly. New industries grew up where they had barely existed before — aircraft in Los Angeles and Seattle, shipyards on the Gulf coast, atomic research at Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

The New Deal had spent around $4 billion a year at peak. War spending reached $98 billion in 1944 alone — roughly twenty times larger. Critics of the New Deal argue this proves Keynesian deficit spending works when it is big enough. Defenders of the New Deal point out that wartime spending also conscripted 12 million men into the armed forces (removing them from the unemployment count) and silenced the Supreme Court and Republican opposition that had hobbled the New Deal in peacetime. Both sides agree that without Pearl Harbor it is unclear when the Depression would have ended.

African-Americans and the Double V Campaign

War production opened doors that had been closed. The Pittsburgh Courier launched the Double V Campaign in 1942: victory against fascism abroad, victory against racism at home. A. Philip Randolph, leader of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, threatened a march on Washington in 1941 unless Roosevelt acted. Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802 in June 1941 banning discrimination in defence industries and creating the Fair Employment Practices Committee — the first federal civil-rights action since Reconstruction.

During the war around 1.5 million African-Americans moved from the South to northern and western cities for war work — the second wave of the Great Migration. Around a million black Americans served in segregated military units. The Tuskegee Airmen, the all-black 332nd Fighter Group, flew over 15,000 missions and earned a battle reputation that contradicted segregationist arguments about black military performance. Yet violence persisted on the home front: the Detroit race riot of June 1943 left 34 people dead, mostly black.

Women on the Home Front

Women filled the gap left by 12 million servicemen. Around 6 million women joined the workforce between 1941 and 1944, many in heavy industry. Rosie the Riveter — the female industrial worker — became a national symbol after a 1943 Norman Rockwell magazine cover and J. Howard Miller’s ‘We Can Do It’ poster. Women welded ships, riveted aircraft and assembled tanks. Around 350,000 women joined the armed forces in non-combat roles such as the WACs (Women’s Army Corps) and WAVES (Navy). Many earned higher wages than they had ever earned before.

The wartime labour gains for women were partial and contested. Female wages in heavy industry were on average around 60% of men’s. Women were widely expected to give back their jobs at the end of the war. Working mothers struggled with limited childcare, although the 1942 Lanham Act funded around 3,000 federal day-care centres. After 1945 around 4 million women were dismissed from war industries to make way for returning servicemen. But the experience of millions of women earning their own wages in skilled industrial work changed expectations that would resurface in the 1960s.

Around 120,000 Japanese-Americans, two-thirds of them US citizens, were forcibly relocated to internment camps under Executive Order 9066 (February 1942) on the grounds of unproven security risk — one of the worst civil-rights violations of the war. Mexican-American workers came north under the 1942 Bracero Programme to fill agricultural labour shortages. Native Americans served in the armed forces in proportionally higher numbers than any other ethnic group; Navajo ‘Code Talkers’ transmitted unbreakable battlefield codes. Rationing of petrol, sugar, butter, meat and clothing reached every household. Around 17 million victory gardens supplied roughly 40% of the nation’s vegetables by 1944.

A Different America in 1945

By the time Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August, the United States had been transformed. National income had roughly doubled. The federal government, which had taken in $7 billion in 1940, took in $50 billion in 1945. The USA emerged as the world’s leading industrial and military power, the only major combatant whose territory had not been bombed. Roosevelt himself died in office on 12 April 1945, weeks before victory in Europe. His successor, Harry Truman, would inherit an economy and a political settlement reshaped by the war and the demands of the millions of Americans who had served, worked or fought in it.

Key Fact

Federal spending rose from $9 billion (1939) to $98 billion (1944) — about twenty times the New Deal’s peak. Conscription removed 12 million men from the unemployment count. The combination of vast deficit spending and the war economy ended the Depression.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 12-mark Period Essay on Roosevelt’s contribution as president, the war years are a strong piece of evidence on both sides: Roosevelt’s political skill in pushing through Lend Lease and rallying the country mattered, but the structural force of war production mattered more for ending unemployment. For 8-mark Explain Effects on the home front, choose two effects (women’s employment, the second Great Migration, federal expansion) and develop each with figures. Avoid the misconception that ‘women got equal rights from the war’ — the gains were real but partial and largely reversed in 1945.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lend Lease (March 1941) ended American neutrality in practice and pumped war orders into US factories before Pearl Harbor; total Lend Lease aid reached around $50 billion.
  • War production — 297,000 aircraft, 86,000 tanks — ended unemployment by 1944 and made the USA the dominant industrial and military power.
  • The home front transformed American society: 1.5 million African-Americans moved north and west, 6 million women joined heavy industry, and Executive Order 8802 was the first federal civil-rights action since Reconstruction.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1944 newspaper article praising Roosevelt’s leadership for delivering economic recovery) and Interpretation B (a 1945 economist’s study arguing only the war ended the Depression). What is the main difference between these views about the recovery?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents recovery as the achievement of Roosevelt’s leadership, his fireside chats, Lend Lease and the war effort.
• Interpretation B presents recovery as the structural effect of vast war spending and conscription rather than political leadership.
• Main difference: A frames recovery as Roosevelt’s personal success; B frames it as the economic consequence of the war regardless of who was president.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1944 newspaper article praising Roosevelt) and Interpretation B (a 1945 economist’s study) give different views about American recovery.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the wartime newspaper aimed to support morale and a fourth Roosevelt term; the economist’s study aimed to analyse the structural drivers of recovery in retrospect.
• They use different evidence — the article cites Roosevelt’s speeches and political decisions; the economist cites federal spending figures and unemployment data.
• They were produced at different points — one in the middle of the war when patriotic framing dominated, one after victory when more sober analysis was possible.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: ‘The Second World War transformed the position of African-Americans in the United States more than the New Deal had ever done.’ How convincing is Interpretation A about the wartime experience of African-Americans?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because Executive Order 8802 (June 1941) banned discrimination in defence industries and created the Fair Employment Practices Committee — the first federal civil-rights action since Reconstruction.
• Convincing because around 1.5 million African-Americans moved north and west in the second Great Migration, taking industrial jobs that the New Deal had not delivered.
• Convincing because the Tuskegee Airmen and the Double V Campaign undermined segregationist arguments and laid foundations for post-war civil-rights demands.
• Less convincing because the armed forces remained segregated and the Detroit race riot of June 1943 (34 dead, mostly black) showed home-front racism intensifying.
• Less convincing because the New Deal had already begun the political shift — the ‘Black Cabinet’, federal employment, and the 1936 black vote moving to the Democrats.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing on economic mobility and federal action; less convincing as a claim of full transformation given continued segregation and violence.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Second World War on women in American society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Mass entry into industrial work — around 6 million women joined the workforce between 1941 and 1944, many welding ships, riveting aircraft and assembling tanks; female employment rose from around 14 million to 19 million.
• Cultural shift symbolised by Rosie the Riveter — the 1943 Norman Rockwell cover and J. Howard Miller’s ‘We Can Do It’ poster reframed female industrial work as patriotic and competent.
• Federal action on childcare — the 1942 Lanham Act funded around 3,000 day-care centres, a small but unprecedented federal presence in family life.
• Partial and reversed gains — female wages in heavy industry averaged around 60% of men’s; around 4 million women were dismissed in 1945–46 to make way for returning servicemen, although the experience of earning skilled wages reshaped expectations that would resurface in the 1960s.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the Second World War ended the Great Depression in the United States.
You may consider:
• Lend Lease and federal war spending
• mobilisation of the workforce, including women and African-Americans.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Lend Lease (March 1941) sent around $50 billion of supplies to Britain and the USSR; American factories started filling with war orders before Pearl Harbor.
• Federal spending rose from $9 billion (1939) to $98 billion (1944) — about twenty times the New Deal’s peak.
• War production figures: 297,000 aircraft, 86,000 tanks, 8,800 warships; the Ford Willow Run plant built a B-24 every 63 minutes at peak.
• Conscription removed 12 million men from the unemployment count; the federal government directly employed around 4 million.
• Women joined the workforce in millions; female employment rose from 14 million to 19 million.
• 1.5 million African-Americans moved to northern and western cities for war work; Executive Order 8802 banned discrimination in defence industries.
• Wages rose around 65%; tax extended to most workers; new industries developed in California, Tennessee and the Gulf coast.
• Limits: rationing, segregated armed forces, Japanese-American internment of 120,000.
• Conclusion: the war ended the Depression because it combined deficit spending, conscription and political consensus that the New Deal had never achieved — structural rather than just political transformation.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Lend-Lease Act of March 1941.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Lend Lease allowed the United States to lend or lease war supplies — weapons, food, oil — to Britain, the Soviet Union and other Allies, without immediate payment.

• Around $50 billion of supplies were shipped under Lend Lease by 1945, with about $32 billion to Britain and around $11 billion to the USSR.
• Roosevelt described the policy as lending a neighbour your hose if their house was on fire, framing it as common-sense self-defence rather than entry into the war.
[Mastering (4): two features clearly identified with developed support. Secure (3): two identified with brief support. Developing (2): one feature developed or two without support. Emerging (1): single thin point.]
